Recent advancements in machine learning have led to the integration of graph neural networks (GNNs) in the subspace learning problem. This issue has garnered significant attention in computer vision, particularly in the field of self-supervised learning. Our work proposes the first time representation learning problem as an optimization issue on a manifold and derives its closed-form solution. By demonstrating the geometric structure of the solution set, we show how GNNs can be leveraged to learn robust subspace representations through message passing. Our method results in SRE, a simple yet effective self-supervised learning method that outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, including SimCLR, on challenging tasks including the ImageNet dataset. Our code is publicly available.

This project focuses on the completeness problem of Sidon sets in finite geometric structures. We have established that certain properties of these sets can be characterized using geometric curves such as hyperbolas and ellipses in a finite affine plane. Additionally, we have created new infinite families of complete Sidon sets by leveraging these geometric properties, including constructions based on elliptical and hyperbolic patterns. We have also derived a new set of values for a particular parameter in these parameters. Furthermore, we have obtained complementary formulas for another set of parameters based on cubic surfaces in a finite geometric space.

We're investigating the impact of different sampling methods when examining large binary matrices. Instead of randomly sampling, we're using a specific non-uniform probability distribution to focus our attention on rows or columns with higher concentrations of 1s. This approach significantly speeds up the computation of important metrics like the imbalance of the matrix, even for extremely large matrices, such as the Genomatrix, a 96000 by 96000 matrix, with just a handful of samples. We compare this scheme to uniform sampling and demonstrate that it yields faster convergence and fewer sampling errors.

The DGLAP evolution equations govern how PDFs change with Q, and by considering PDFs at various Q values, researchers have a broader understanding of their behavior. Although not directly involved in the PDF fitting process, DGLAP evolution still plays a crucial role, as measured Q^2 data (like PDFs at different Q^2 values) are evolved to one universal scale (Q_0) and then compared. In this work, we explore how incorporating the DGLAP evolution directly into the fitting procedure could be beneficial and improve our knowledge of PDFs. We examine two potential approaches to achieve this and assess their potential.

Our open-source data mining and analysis framework, ELKI, enables efficient computation of state-of-the-art algorithms on both core and advanced techniques through a range of core components. These components include parallel processing capabilities, a load model that accelerates many algorithms, and an approach to estimate the density of datasets. Additionally, we have integrated the capacity to compare results and extend the framework's functionality by introducing new algorithms.

We developed an advanced numerical model to simulate the behavior of a microresonator based on four-wave mixing processes. The driving force of our simulation includes the influence of the pump's sidebands. The outcomes in a microcomb's spectrum depended on two key variables: the position of the pump's sidebands and their width. We demonstrated that when the pump's bandwidth was narrower, the spacing between pump frequencies had a significant impact on the spectrum. We also discovered the existence of a critical point where the pump's bandwidth started to influence the order in which spectral lines appeared. Additionally, we observed self-phase modulation effects on individual line components and noted differences in the power and broadening of these lines.

For any infinite discrete group G, any of its non-trivial conjugation-invariant normal subgroups is selected at random using G's word probability measure. The resulting random subgroup will be both weakly mixing and faithful if G is either abelian or has finitely many conjugacy classes. This general result is applied in specific cases, such as showing that the group Z ⊕ F_n has a characteristically weakly mixing and faithful random subgroup, while torsion-abelian groups of finite rank show similar properties.

Deep neural networks can be understood through a kernel method during training, which relies on the "neural tangent kernel". However, this approach has limitations due to varying parameter scales in deep networks. To bypass these restrictions, "quasi neural networks" were introduced, which decouple their output parameters and allow for exploration of the neural tangent kernel's behavior with different scaling. These networks have a more manageable "gradient flow" dynamic and their tangent kernel shows an exponential decay, enabling analysis of their testing error and training dynamics. The study also reveals a "generalization phase transition" in such networks and provides insights into the influence of initialization on their learning performance, along with an exploration of the effects of a residual term in the neural tangent kernel.

A requirement that a bulk entropy meets is directly derived from these constraints place a significant restriction on the associated boundary entropes. This imposes a significant restriction on a broad category of boundary entropes, with varying levels of severity. A range of information measures are examined to assess the impact of monogamy on bulk entropies, resulting in a direct consequence on associated boundary entropies. The extensive application of monogamy of mutual information across various holographic formulae gives rise to a broad and diverse set of requirements for boundary entropes in diverse scenarios.

A novel probabilistic framework is introduced for a broad class of solvable interaction-round-a-face models. The local state probabilities are expressed via a generalized algebraic rule of the branching type, with two key examples identified. It is also shown that these probabilities conform to the quadratic invariant property. Additionally, certain thermodynamic characteristics, including the free energy, are investigated, particularly in one-dimensional scenarios, with the resulting free energy landscape being continuous. Moreover, new summary formulas are formulated. The method's validity is confirmed through the exact calculation of the transfer matrix for the restricted non-crossing Ising model.

We investigated the effect of integrating various stabilization methods for compressed sensing, a popular signal recovery technique. We found that combining different stabilization procedures can lead to more effective results, as the individual methods' limitations can be compensated for, thus enhancing overall performance. We proposed a new method that merges $\ell_1$ and iterative soft-thresholding procedures, demonstrating that the method's outcomes converge to those of the $\ell_1$ method while incorporating the performance benefits of the iterative soft-thresholding procedure. We also created an modified version of this method, incorporating a procedure to detect and correct incorrect signals prior to each iteration of the algorithm, resulting in significantly improved accuracy compared to the original method, especially for signals with a high sparsity level. Performance assessments were carried out using both exact and approximate messages passing, with the latter incorporating the procedure to correct and stabilize inaccurate signals before each iteration of the algorithm, resulting in a more efficient and reliable signal recovery algorithm.

A common technique in astronomical data analysis is combining individual images of the same celestial object into a single co-added image. This is typically done using linear addition which preserves the object's original shape and allows for accurate photometry. However, using nonlinear co-addition algorithms such as median or clipped-mean can distort stellar profiles by not maintaining the point spread function, a problem that is less relevant for planetary objects due to their extended nature. This research investigates the effect of nonlinear co-addition on stellar photometry using DCOSPS, an automated photometry pipeline. The study finds that median and clipped-mean algorithms introduce significant residuals in stellar profiles, resulting in incorrect photometry. In contrast, the mode estimator provides a more accurate non-linear estimator that maintains stellar profile consistency. A practical solution is presented for applying the mode estimator in stellar photometry, which improves the precision of photometric measurements.

We introduce chordal Schramm-Löwner evolution with reflection and demonstrate
its equivalence to an evolutionary system of imaginary surfaces. This gives
rise to a family of surfaces for each time value, where any two surface
configurations are related by a local inversion transformation. Image of a
chordal Schramm-Löwner evolution curve under reflection gives an imaginary
surface trace. We investigate local behavior near the endpoints of the evolution
curve and show that confidence bands can be constructed. These are formed by
interconnecting the traces of multiple reflection curves and provide a region
where the imaginary surface is guaranteed to be present. A software tool,
reflectLE, has been developed to visualize chordal Schramm-Löwner evolution
curves and the associated imaginary surfaces by taking multiple simulations of
chordal Schramm-Löwner evolution and their reflections as band edges.

For the 3D Navier-Stokes equations with small constant viscosity, we derive an upper limit on an infinite time regularity norm of the smooth solution, expressed solely in terms of the maximum norm of the initial data, specifically $\|e\|_{L^\infty([0,\infty);L^2(\mathbb R^3))}$.

To assess the computational complexity of circuit models utilizing quantum advantage, Verification of Computational Results in Quantum circuits (CVQC) is essential. Currently, the most effective interactive proof strategies rely on quantum resources from the prover, limiting their applicability in scenarios where quantum assistance is unavailable. This research introduces a novel probabilistic cross-verification protocol employing Bell measurement and achieves an O(log N) quantum communication complexity, offering theoretical support for employing classical resources to enhance the prover's output reliability. Notably, this protocol can double the verification speed when the prover produces correct results 75% or more frequently, and our experiments demonstrate its practical feasibility on superconducting quantum processors.

A cell shape synthesis model can greatly enhance cell-based biomorphological analysis and inform various applications such as tracking, segmentation, and signal extraction from biomolecular images. We approach the complex task of generating cell shapes as a process of transforming uniform noise into actual cell shapes. To achieve this, we develop a new deep generative model for cell shape synthesis, rooted in signal processing principles. This new model, called deep generative cell morphing, utilizes a specialized training strategy that involves a uniform noise input and gradually introduces real cell shape features. Through extensive testing on an extensive, manually curated cell shape dataset consisting of tracked nuclear shapes, our proposed method demonstrates superior performance in generating nuclear shapes in comparison to existing synthesis models.

Researchers in reinforcement learning (RL) have been investigating the concept of
memories and their role in RL policies for a considerable period of time.
A recent breakthrough by Dabney et al. revealed that neural networks with
recurrent layers can utilize these memories to enhance performance on
geometric tasks. However, a crucial question remains: are these memories
actually beneficial or do they introduce noise that hampers performance?
In this research, we conducted a systematic analysis of memory features using
various datasets and RCWQ environments. We found that the characteristics
of these memories have a direct impact on performance, with persistent features
consistently improving outcomes across all settings.
Furthermore, we developed feature selection algorithms to identify the most
effective memory features and subsequently on a primary benchmark found
exceptional results, outperforming the original policy by a significant margin.
Our approach not only sheds light on the nature of memories in RL policies but
also provides a new perspective on utilizing them to optimize performance.

A revised version of the Newtonian ECMC algorithm is presented, designed to tackle issues of dynamical arrest in three-dimensional dipolar models. In its original form, the ECMC algorithm integrates Monte-Carlo and molecular dynamics by selecting a pair of particles and attempting to match their velocities through rejection-and-acceptance process. Its efficiency, however, is limited by the probability of particle selection, which becomes particularly low when particles slow down. To address this limitation, the Newtonian ECMC was designed, where only faster particles participate in the exchange process. This approach significantly reduces the risk of dynamical arrest, which affects the original ECMC. By integrating the modified algorithm with a simulation of 3D dipolar aluminum atoms, we demonstrate an enhancement of approximately two orders of magnitude over the standard ECMC method, without compromising detailed balance or ergodicity.

To enhance the accuracy of sound event detection, various techniques have been developed, including methods to expand the training dataset to overcome issues like limited data and overfitting. In this study, we focus on evaluating the effectiveness of data augmentation methods in enhancing a neural network-based sound event detection system, building on its prior success in single-source sound recognition tasks. We experiment with applying time, frequency, and neural methods of data augmentation to the training data and assess their impact in a large-scale challenge, the DCASE 2020.

We introduce a novel multi-user detection method based on superposition, which yields considerable improvements in performance and complexity compared to existing approaches. This method also exhibits a superposition property that enables various applications, such as federated learning and non-orthogonal multiple access. Furthermore, we develop a practical algorithm for enforcing the superposition property, which can be applied to any existing approach, and experimentally demonstrate the feasibility of superposition-based learning and communication systems.

Recent advances in signal detection and estimation leverage set-theoretic
methods, such as geometric level sets, in the frequency-time spectrogram
representation. To classify a signal, the algorithm determines which predefined
sets the spectrum occupies. Researchers employ various distance measures and
optimization methods to resolve this problem efficiently. Nonetheless,
optimizing geometric distance measures may result in a local optimum and the
existence of multiple sets necessitates resolving numerous subproblems.
Furthermore, measuring the spectrum's intersection with multiple geometric
sets individually does not always guarantee a correct classification.
To address these challenges, this paper proposes an area metric measure on
$\mathbb{R}^2$ and investigates its suitability for spectrogram analysis.
Using this metric, this work presents a novel approach to signal classification
and detection that utilizes a single optimization problem, ensuring accurate
results. Introducing a novel intersection measure, this method evaluates the
intersection of a spectrogram with multiple geometric sets simultaneously,
thus avoiding multiple local optimizations. Experimental outcomes on a wide
range of signals demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing
algorithms, particularly in speech spectrogram analysis.

We introduce an innovative strategy for aligning multiple clusters within a system's dynamics by leveraging a novel concept of generalized phase alignment. This approach allows us to formulate an optimization-based method for dynamically adjusting coupling parameters across different systems, ensuring synchronized cluster behavior. Specifically, our research focuses on characterizing aligned states in complex networks composed of identical systems featuring unique unstable periodic orbits. By employing local adaptation mechanisms, our proposed method can generate synchronized clusters without necessitating a globally uniform coupling strength. Moreover, our findings demonstrate the ability to simultaneously produce various synchronized clusters and explore the concurrent alignment of distinct unstable periodic orbits within the same network.

We introduce an advanced module called the Actuation Module for Particle Dynamics (AMP), which is now integrated into the COMSOL Multiphysics 6.0 update. AMP enables the creation of comprehensive simulations of particles in complex physical systems by facilitating interactions with the computational mesh and other COMSOM Multiphysics models. Using the AMP module, users can accurately model the behavior of particles within their system context, including factors like fluid dynamics, electrostatics, adhesion forces, gravitational forces, drag, and buoyancy. AMP offers two distinct methods for spatial discretization of particles - the Lagrangian approach, which tracks individual particles, and the Eulerian approach, which simulates particle layers on surfaces. For further details on applying particle dynamics simulations, please refer to the "Particle Dynamics" model reference manual.

A pioneering PRL article introduced an electrical circuit designed to measure the trajectory of a single electron in real-time, marking a significant breakthrough in measurement technology. This innovation enabled researchers to explore thermodynamic investigations of individual electrons and opened up various avenues for exploration, such as information processing and quantum-phenomenon emulation. Building upon this circuit's rationale, this study presents a theoretical investigation into designing an information engine that operates under continuous measurement conditions. This approach represents a substantial advancement over conventional thermal machines that rely on discrete measurement cycles. Our proposed model features a two-level system coupled to a resistor, subject to continuous measurement and a state-dependent external force, which can be adjusted in real-time to perform useful work. This theoretical framework can be implemented using modern nanotechnology and verified using state-of-the-art measurement circuits. The results show that the proposed engine achieves optimal efficiency at finite power output when subjected to continuous measurement, showcasing continuous measurement's inherent advantages.

Research into the impacts of El Niño and La Niña has evolved from examining distinct weather conditions to exploring a more nuanced spectrum of different "flavors" within these phenomena. These variations can result in divergent precipitation patterns, leading to significant economic and life-threatening consequences. A recent study analyzed the relationship between this spectrum of different El Niño and La Niña states and regional precipitation, utilizing a sophisticated statistical approach. The research identified a multi-flavored pattern in precipitation anomalies across the Pacific, Indian, and African oceans. Evidence of this relationship was found in long-term climate records, with a notable finding that the different states of El Niño and La Niña exhibit distinct precipitation effects. This discovery holds far-reaching implications, underscoring the need to accurately represent various aspects of ENSO in climate models and global warming projections.

The upper mass limit of black holes in the universe is influenced by their formation and feeding processes, especially their initial masses. We've investigated how variations in the seed mass of black holes, either small or large, affect their ultimate mass limits. Small seed black holes, formed from gas inflows in the early universe, are thought to outgrow a certain mass, after which their growth is impeded by instability. In contrast, we've found that large seed black holes, formed from the direct collapse of gas, inherit a mass which, although subject to the same stabilizing effects, will be elevated by a factor of approximately 10 to 20 compared to smaller seed black holes, thus potentially overcoming the mass limit imposed on smaller seed black holes and thereby raising the overall mass limit of black holes in the universe. Our findings are based on a theoretical framework and will need to be verified through future observations.

In the context of two-dimensional systems with multiple orbitals on a honeycomb lattice, research has consistently shown that correlation effects are induced by flat bands. This occurs particularly in the presence of specific orbital interactions and orbital ordering. However, studies have also suggested that the geometric arrangement of the lattice may play a more significant role in inducing these effects. To explore this hypothesis, we investigate flat band-induced correlation in a square lattice with two orbitals per site. Our study demonstrates that the arrangement of orbital dipoles along bonds can lead to an effective inter-site exchange interaction through an超交换 mechanism. As a result, this gives rise to an effective spin exchange that is an函数 of the orbital arrangement. Ultimately, this leads to an ultra-exchange coupling that is an函数 of nearest neighbor orbital arrangements.

Understanding which genetic variations lead to specific traits is a critical aspect of medical research. However, the relationship between genetic variations and traits is complex, influenced by the sequences of relevant proteins and following distinct patterns for different traits. We developed a novel approach to identify variations in proteins that affect specific traits, using information from organisms both with and without a certain trait. This score is calculated based on how often each amino acid appears in proteins linked to a trait compared to those that don't. When combined with existing data, this approach can effectively identify genes connected to traits and their underlying mechanisms. For example, applying this method to two well-studied proteins, hemoglobin and insulin, revealed distinct patterns of amino acid variations associated with different traits. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that the genetic variations affecting specific traits are more concentrated in regions influenced by specific regulatory elements than previously documented.

We have found all 2-designs where the number of points is a prime power and the automorphism group has a prime number of cycles of length prime p. Specifically, we have confirmed a long-standing hypothesis about these designs, called the Crq-conjecture, and our findings reveal the presence of three distinct families of 2-designs, including projective planes, unit circles, and specific families identified by crq. Notably, our research also led to the discovery of new examples of planes and other planes of translation type.

We analyze the Coulomb correlation energy in electronic systems confined within a 2D cavity using a unique approach. This quasi-non-perturbative method is grounded in the link between Coulomb correlation effects and the Coulomb interaction's informational entropy characteristics. Successful applications of similar information-theory-based approaches to approximate the Coulomb correlation energy have historically been confined to 3D systems. In this study, theoretical predictions from our approach are compared with those from quantum Monte Carlo simulations to validate the findings. Notably, the informational entropy-derived estimates closely align with the quantum Monte Carlo results, particularly in the strong correlation regime. This new technique holds promise for its application to model and simulate a broad spectrum of quasi-2D confined electronic systems.

This study investigates velocity dispersion measurements in wide binary star systems, comparing and analyzing three datasets, which include: (1) Galactic field wide binaries from the first Gaia catalog; (2) Galactic halo wide binaries from the second Gaia catalog; (3) and velocity fields derived from second Gaia catalog fields of 10x10 degrees. For each dataset, we calculate one-dimensional and three-dimensional velocity dispersions, focusing on the influence of using precise line velocities. We find that employing line velocities significantly enhances the accuracy of one-dimensional velocity dispersion, but has a negligible effect on three-dimensional velocity dispersion due to its reliance on radial and tangential velocity differences. However, the inclusion of velocity scatter induced by line-of-sight velocity errors leads to an overestimation of three-dimensional velocity dispersion. Ultimately, the choice of dataset and radial distance can greatly affect three-dimensional velocity dispersion and wide binary star parameters such as mass function and density, underscoring the importance of selecting an appropriate sample and controlling for radial distance.

In multiplicative linear logic, a well-established link exists between the logical content of proof structures and the concept of ideal representations, initially introduced by Belin and Melli\'es. Ideal representations serve as a means to equate proof structures and a mechanism to assign meaning to them. Building on this connection, we develop a method to evaluate how closely an ideal representation aligns with its corresponding proof structure. This approach relies on special ideal representations called minimal ideal representations, which we show exist uniquely for any proof group. We then apply this approach to define a novel metric on the set of proof groups, enabling the measurement of the similarity between them.

We investigate the application of deep learning in forecasting the synchronization of two time series of varying complexity, using a Cointegration Deep Network. This model harnesses the principles of cointegration to achieve a long-term synchronization of the two time series, which, although not directly relevant to our objective, facilitates our experiment. We assess the synchronization of the two series before and after applying the Cointegration Deep Network by evaluating the zero-lag cross-correlation of their residuals for 70 pairs of financial assets, drawn from 7 distinct asset classes, consisting of a diverse mixture of linear and high-dimensional nonlinear relationships. Notably, our results indicate a substantial 10 to 50 percent improvement in correlation for the majority of pairs, demonstrating the robustness of our method in handling multiple series of nonlinear relationships.

The concept of nanothermometry has emerged as a highly accurate tool for monitoring temperature changes at the nanoscale. Recent advancements suggest that quantum effects may also be leveraged to manipulate reaction processes. We theorize that coupling a vibrational mode with a quantum state could enable more precise control over a reaction's energy barrier and potentially lower the activation energy. To validate this hypothesis, we combine ab-initio and cavity quantum electrodynamics simulations to study the influence of coupling a C-H stretch with an off-resonant microwave cavity on the barrier to proton transfer in the simple molecule, methanol. By adjusting coupling and dissipation rates, different reaction characteristics can be achieved. Strong pure state coupling may enhance selectivity in complex molecules by further lowering the reaction's energy barrier, while coupling with Fano resonances offers an alternative strategy that could be applicable to a wider range of molecules. Our findings indicate that this approach might one day enable the manipulation of more intricate molecules beyond the limitations of zero-point motion.

Online advertisers seek to maximize their ROI by incentivizing user clicks.
While Machine Learning models can accurately predict user clicks, they tend to
overlook the visual appeal of ads. To promote more engaging and visually
aligned ad presentations, we need to prioritize the features that attract user
interest. In this study, we examine the impact of visual ad identifiers on
click-through rate (CTR) prediction models. These IDs serve as a pivotal
ingredient in supervised learning models aimed at predicting CTR. We propose
a novel approach for generating ad IDs that leverages pairwise historical
click data. By doing so, our method maximizes the separation of ads with
distinct users. We assess our method using a publicly accessible dataset, comparing
the efficacy of our proposed approach to existing techniques. The experimental
results indicate a notable improvement in model accuracy when utilizing our
suggested IDs.

Business processes in organizations frequently involve concurrent activities that need to be managed efficiently. Business Process Management systems provide a framework for overseeing these processes, ensuring that activities conform to established rules. Although BPM systems can enforce constraints on activity execution, they often struggle with concurrent activities that may lead to unnecessary pauses. To address this limitation, we propose an approach that incorporates constraints on the number of simultaneous activities within a business process. Based on Petri nets, our method ensures that constraints are respected during process execution, that violations can be detected and that enforcement actions are only applied when necessary. We demonstrate the feasibility of our approach through a practical example and evaluate its performance through timing experiments.

A numerical model called FIRE-AOD is introduced to predict the optimal conditions for detecting ash aerosol optical depth (AOD) from satellite imagery in the presence of wildfires. This model is developed with a Bayesian framework, ensuring transparency and incorporating the necessary adjustments for radiative transfer modeling and temporal/diurnal variations inherent to ash plumes. By applying this method, FIRE-AOD successfully captures the diverse characteristics of ash plumes, from opaque to translucent, and predicts their optimal detection times. By analyzing over 1000 satellite images of 13 global wildfires, FIRE-AOD predicts the best and forbidden periods for detecting AOD, with results closely aligning with in-situ ash concentration measurements from aircraft. Moreover, FIRE-AOD's predictive capabilities are robust across different wildfires, fire sizes, and diurnal cycles. Consequently, FIRE-AOD is a valuable tool for satellite-based ash retrieval, as it identifies both feasible and impractical periods for accurate AOD retrieval, with its open-source availability promoting consistent and reliable ash retrievals.

A significant concern with location-based services is the balance between utility and privacy. Two existing approaches either disregard conditional dependencies in data or utilize an overly conservative assumption of independence, resulting in suboptimal utility or excessive privacy loss. In this study, we introduce a novel framework that strikes a balance between utility and privacy loss by considering dependent data and incorporating it into the differential privacy mechanism. Furthermore, we develop two specific techniques for handling dependent data: the first merges dependent data points, while the second accounts for the distribution of dependent data. We also propose an adaptive framework for handling dynamic data dependence, specifically in real-time applications like navigation. By designing two techniques, one that tracks transitions and another that tracks distributions, we demonstrate the framework's effectiveness through comparative analysis of two case studies, including real-world data from a mobile robot and a navigation service.

The connectivity between distinct brain regions is used to assess individual variability, differentiate between patients and controls, and identify the effects of interventions. However, an underlying issue exists: inter-site influences on this functional connectivity may impede our ability to draw valid conclusions. This study investigates how inter-site effects impact our ability to detect individual, group variations, and distinguish disease states. Using resting-state fMRI data from brain imaging centers across the US, the researchers analyzed the inter-site effects on network overlap and connectivity patterns. They found that while site differences are substantial, they do not consistently exceed individual differences. However, inter-site effects can sometimes exceed patient-control differences. The researchers developed a novel approach to eliminate inter-site effects and demonstrated its benefits. By removing inter-site effects, the researchers improved our ability to differentiate between individuals and identified the effects of disease and interventions. This new approach may be particularly valuable in studies focusing on high-stakes conditions.

Building on efforts to derive concentration of measure inequalities for systems with constraints, we explore the connection between the decay of the flow's heat kernel and these inequalities, given that both rely on a common underlying structure - the flow's geometric characteristics. We also derive an inequality of Talagrand-type, combining both entropy and distance characteristics, from which the concentration of measure inequality can be inferred.

Our proposed method incorporates an innovative encoding technique into pre-trained language models to accommodate code-switched text. This technique conveys information about which language a token belongs to, allowing the underlying model to make more informed predictions. In this study, we explore two distinct approaches: one that encodes language identity into a specific dimension of the token embedding and another that incorporates language identity as additional information in the model input. Experimental results show that introducing position-wise language identifiers significantly improves code-switched text processing, outperforming the base model by 2.6% in Indian language text and achieving better or comparable performance on English and Spanish.

To study and superconduct in unexplored regions and substances, researchers need for powerful, easily controlled, and compact methods of manipulating superconducting materials, which high magnetic fields offer. We investigated the superconducting properties of H$_3$S under a high hydrostatic pressure of 35 GPa and ultra-high purity conditions. Our experiments revealed a significant isotope coefficient variation with pressure, likely due to the influence of pressure media. Consequently, at extremely high pressures, Isotope effect becomes negligible, enabling accurate measurements free from mass-dependent effects. Our findings also indicate that hydrogen isotopes exhibit distinct behaviors in the H$_3$S isotope effect coefficient. Our research has made it possible to accurately measure the isotope coefficient in H$_3$S at very high pressures for the first time, and our results have implications for understanding the superconducting properties of other materials such as FeSe and MgB$_2$.

We develop a probabilistic framework for phenotypic evolution, drawing from the works of S. Wright, D. Fisher, and others, to investigate the limited yet valuable connection between average effects of gene substitution and large-scale phenotypic changes. This investigation is conducted within the context of empirical studies, such as the study of yeast evolution, where numerous gene-substitution events have occurred, rendering the concept of gene-substitution effects insufficient to describe overall evolutionary dynamics.

This paper examines the role of closed-loop feedback in improving robustness
for models trained via simulation-to-real simulation (S2R1) simulation to real
robot (S2R2) (S2R2) deployment. Specifically, we investigate the effects of
delayed state-sensitivities on the walking performance of a controlled robotic
system, using a passive dynamic walker (PDW) design as our test subject. We
compare the open, pre-programmed, closed and predictive control loops. We find
that predictive control, implemented in real-time with feedback and state
delay compensation, best preserves the walking dynamics similar to the open
loop, particularly important during the stance phase where immediate closed
loop feedback is ineffective. We demonstrate the predictive model's capacity
for tracking delayed bipedal robot states and predict future states to minimize
control delays.

We present a novel learning-based pipeline for absolute camera pose estimation that utilizes pre-defined viewpoints and on-board pose data to produce robust descriptors. These descriptors are then used in a descriptor matching approach to calculate the camera pose. The proposed method demonstrates resilience in challenging situations such as weather conditions, distinct scene configurations, and changes in the number of descriptors. In scenarios without prior pose information, the camera pose is calculated based on the best descriptor matches after aligning the descriptors. When available, on-board pose data is used to adjust the camera pose by applying a rotation and potentially a scale factor from the estimated pose. Notably, the proposed method is completely keypoint-free, leading to enhanced descriptor efficiency. The framework has been integrated into SOFT, a visual positioning system, and has proven to provide more reliable descriptor descriptors, resulting in significantly improved camera pose estimation performance.

Most existing approaches to federated learning adopt a centralized and semi-supervised strategy, aiming to establish a single model that serves all clients with minimal data annotations. This model struggles to accommodate personalized needs of clients with limited data. To address this, we have developed a new personalized semi-supervised learning approach for clients with incomplete data. We introduce a novel data augmentation technique to maintain the model's consistency with clients' original data distribution. This novel paradigm enables each client to train its own local model using both its labeled and anonymized anonymized data. The results show that our method significantly outperforms existing federated learning approaches on datasets like EMNIST, DNS, and JODI. Specifically, we observed a relative improvement of 14.77% on EMNIST, 10.22% on DNS, and 6.13% on JODI.

Following a neutron star disruption in a binary neutron star - black hole merger, we observed the binary black hole - neutron star merger for the first time. Simulations were conducted with various initial binary orbital periods ranging from a few days to a week. These orbital periods were varied to mimic different stellar evolution histories. Our findings indicate that, following the disruption of the neutron star, the binary black hole - neutron star merger occurs within a timespan of days to weeks. During this time, the binary black hole spins remain largely unchanged. As the binary black hole spins decrease by orders of magnitude, a significantly larger disk forms around the black hole, resulting in a more substantial mass and accretion disk. Consequently, this leads to a more intense post-merger X-ray flare emission. Furthermore, the binary black hole with a smaller initial orbital period tends to produce a more luminous and longer-lasting X-ray flare in the post-merger phase. Ultimately, we note that, following a binary neutron star - black hole merger, an established black hole spin can still produce detectable X-ray flare emission due to a substantial accretion disk.

We establish a structure across the full class of compact Riemann surfaces of a given genus. This involves defining'sleaves', subsets within this class that are locally uniform, via constructing an extensive atlas of Del-Magnago, Lando, and Zvonkin's compactified Riemann surfaces with fixed moduli and invariants. Additionally, we determine the significance of the initial Mumford-Morita-Miller class, identifying its nontriviality on the first level and defining its cohomology basis for the remaining genuses.

This study provides a detailed explanation of the Markov processes that possess invariance under time reversal with distinct quasi-stationary distributions. Under specific ergodicity and symmetry conditions, we establish the existence of a distinct quasi-stationary distribution and exponential convergence. These conditions are significant as they are essential for the distinct quasi-stationary distribution's existence and can be interpreted through a detailed balance principle. The research expands on the work of [K. P. Bergner and B. G. Courbet, Time-reversal invariant Markov processes with distinct quasi-stationary distributions. arXiv:2101.01003], which focused on ergodicity under time reversal invariance.

By employing an experimentally achievable standing wave pattern, we can manipulate the behavior of dielectric particles on the surface of graphene. Adjusting the chemical potential of the graphene allows us to establish a stable equilibrium position for these particles. Moreover, this technique enables the precise and contact-free positioning and alignment of the particles, a capability that can be effectively utilized for various applications, including the development of advanced devices based on graphene and the creation of innovative biological and medical treatments.

Patients who experience longer-than-expected delays in treatment at Emergency Departments (EDs) are more likely to experience subsequent delays or treatment disruptions. One such disruption is a patient's readmission or a revisit to the ED within 30 days. This study investigates whether increasing actual treatment duration would contribute to these short-term outcomes within a large health system comprising 11 hospitals and over 1 million visits over 10 years. Using a difference-in-differences approach and actual patient data, researchers simulated the effect of adding 30 minutes to average treatment duration. This addition was unevenly distributed among hospitals before the intervention, allowing for a valid comparison. After the intervention, average treatment duration at participating hospitals increased by 20 minutes. In contrast, average duration increased by 29 minutes at non-intervening hospitals. As a result, the analysis revealed that this increase in treatment duration led to a 10 percentage point rise in both revisit and readmission rates, equating to a 10% relative increase, while controlling for various factors. This observed correlation suggests the potential for the "sick role" disruption to occur, where the extended treatment duration may have negative effects on patients.

This study investigates how varying levels of cognitive processing and the distribution of task complexities impact decision-making strategies and overall performance in a multi-agent system. A computational model is used to simulate different cognitive processing levels and compare their performance across various task difficulty settings. The results show that, when tasks are randomly selected, different cognitive processing levels produce similar overall performance. However, when easier tasks are prioritized, more advanced cognitive processing leads to a notable improvement in performance.

An comprehensive examination of the background influences on the vCoefficients measurement through two-body charge-dependent correlations is conducted. Research reveals that backgrounds which respect local charge conservation, such as conservation within jets or sub-jets, have the capability to mimic the charge-sensitive signal of pseudoscalar decays and distort measurements. An essential observation is that differences in local charge-conservation correlations between major backgrounds and photons increase with rapidity separation between the photon and the corresponding hadron. In a simulated photon sample aligning with ATLAS data at 13 TeV, local background influences significantly outweigh predictions from charge-sensitive pseudoscalar decays at rapidity differences greater than 1.2, underscoring a necessary thorough treatment of local charge-conservation backgrounds in future measurements of the anisotropic flow coefficient and rapidity ranges used in such studies.

Online fundraising has become a significant tool for funding various causes and initiatives, making it crucial to identify key elements that contribute to its success. However, many existing studies only concentrate on the financial or promotional aspects, leaving a knowledge gap. We address this issue by applying machine learning techniques to discover new, non-obvious insights into the dynamics of Canadian crowd dynamics. We develop predictive models for reach and success, using a combination of crowd, project creator, and campaign features. Our results reveal that unique aspects of the crowd dynamics are more informative than project creator or campaign features. We also discover that the initial aspects of a campaign have a substantial impact on its future behavior and final outcome. Our research enables stakeholders to make more informed decisions, which can improve the overall online fundraising experience.

In a novel fusion of Big Data and machine learning, the integration of IoT devices and cloud computing facilitates the analysis of massive datasets. Nevertheless, the associated data storage and processing are vulnerable to cyber threats, including network intrusions. To address this, researchers have developed Big Data-based machine learning models for network intrusion detection. While effective, these models have limitations, including the security risks of sharing sensitive data. To overcome these limitations, we propose a federated learning framework for network intrusion detection. This approach allows organizations to collaborate on the shared data without exposing their private datasets. Two distributed classifiers, K-Nearest Neighbor and Multi-Layer Perceptron, are utilized. These classifiers are trained locally using a stochastic gradient descent algorithm and their weights are then aggregated using a federated averaging method. The proposed method is tested using the NSL-KDD dataset, yielding a 98% average accuracy with the MLP federated classifier showing superior performance. This result demonstrates the effectiveness of our method, which can be extended to other domains as well.

The RASP algorithm is designed to expedite various robotic tasks by leveraging parallel processing and the utilization of multiple power robots to accomplish a single task simultaneously. RASP's efficiency improvements are most noticeable in applications that were previously limited by execution time, and its development is inspired by the sequential version of the RAM problem, with the addition of a spatial component to account for movement within a tree structure. This paper examines tasks suitable for execution using RASP, implements the model on a simulated environment using the MATLAB/Gazebo platform, and analyzes execution times to demonstrate RASP's effectiveness. Additionally, the paper outlines strategies for integrating RASP into different types of robotic applications.

The choice of semiconductor and gate materials significantly affects device performance and thus needs to be considered in advanced technology development. In this research, we used the empirical tight-binding method to investigate the effects of replacing silicon with germanium and using magnetic metals as gate materials. We found that mismatched gate and semiconductor materials result in higher mobility due to the empirical tight-binding method's ability to accurately capture magnetic properties. Furthermore, we observed that vertical device orientation yields even higher mobility gains. Ultimately, we identified several combinations of semiconductor and gate materials that meet the requirements for technologies with mV/K thresholds.

In certain types of coupled oscillator networks, a particular phenomenon called group synchronization, a significant aspect of their stability landscape, has been extensively studied. However, a significant gap exists in our understanding of how miniaturization affects this phenomenon. Our research aims to fill this knowledge void by providing insights into the impact of small deviations in system parameters on the stability of this coupled oscillator phenomenon. Our findings are based on multiple approaches, including mathematical reduction and numerical simulations, which reveal that group stability can be analyzed through multiple eigenvalues even in the presence of these small perturbations. Furthermore, our study demonstrates that these perturbations do not influence the directions of these combined eigenvalues, but they do affect their multiplicity by reducing it to a single dimension, a crucial discovery with significant implications for experimental verification.

This research examines the search results generated by a set of popular search engines Western users rely on for navigating the web. These search outputs were analyzed for the presence of Chinese-owned companies, with a particular focus on Alibaba and its subsidiary YouTube. By running searches using commonly recommended keywords, our study discovered that only one out of nine research engines examined - Ecosia - failed to showcase Alibaba's properties. Notably, our analysis revealed that YouTube was universally present in the search outputs of the ten search engines, with all other related videos, tutorials, and comments also stemming from this platform. These findings are further discussed through underlying political implications and our study is made accessible to the public to promote transparency.

We've investigated the behavior of the zeta function in relation to a monodromy defect in a scalar field system governed by the equation u = κr^-4(4κ)^n. The defect causes the derivative of u with respect to r to diverge as r approaches zero. Although this presents challenges, it turns out that the self-adjoint operator associated with this defect has a discrete spectrum, and thus a delta function in the zeta function is not an issue. However, changing the monodromy defect does significantly affect the zeta function trace term. Notably, for certain values of the monodromy defect's index, the behavior of u with respect to the defect index is smooth, and this has direct implications for how heat kernel coefficients behave in relation to the defect index.

We examine an elliptic curve $E$ over a cubic Galois extension $K$ of $\mathbb{Q}$ with a $K$-rational point of order 13. In case $K$ is the Galois closure of a $\mathbb{Q}$-quartic biquadratic field, we identify $E$ as being isomorphic to curve 13274.13.1.1 over $\mathbb{Q}$. If instead $K$ is the Galois closure of a $\mathbb{Q}$-quartic non-biquadratic field, we identify two groups of such curves. In the first set, we find curve 13274.13.1.1 is again a member, while the second group features an additional element, either curve 13274.13.2.1 or 13274.13.3.1, depending on specific conditions of the field.

We have developed an examination of the operation of CBR, VB-NR, and VRB protocols under an independent, identically distributed packet delay assumption. This analysis divides the operation into four domains based on packet delay: small, locally delay-dependent, globally delay-dependent, and large. It is determined that each region has distinct efficiency expectations for the three protocols. For NR-VB and NR-VRB, we create decentralized variants, VB and VRB, applicable to packet switching systems.

This paper investigates the application of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in the realm of semi-supervised node classification. It specifically focuses on the potential of leveraging large amounts of unlabeled data. We analyze the effect of a commonly used pseudo-labeling method and its implications on the effectiveness of GNNs. The unpreserved classification targets of the initial batch by this approach are a concern. Moreover, existing methods that correct the pseudo-labels either correct them for the entire graph or solely based on the GNN's final output. However, such corrections may not adequately address the problem. As such, we introduce new methods that correct pseudo-labels based on both the GNN's intermediate and final representations. These methods provide more accurate correction of the pseudo-labels and thus improve the overall classification performance. Experimental results on various real-world datasets demonstrate the superior accuracy of our proposed methods.

This study presents a novel deep learning approach called PatchNet, designed for
video object detection in compressed videos. Utilizing a convolutional neural
network with an attention mechanism, PatchNet can process low-resolution video
metadata. The network integrates the Gates Network to enhance memory efficiency
by dynamically allocating memory based on input complexity. With a Split-Merge
module, PatchNet achieves high computational speed without compromising
performance. By embedding the Gates Network and Split-Merge module within
Conv2D layers, PatchNet optimizes its parameter count. Evaluation of PatchNet
using the Things7 and FLAME datasets demonstrates its superior accuracy
when compared to MobileNetV2, while outperforming YOLO-V3 in terms of speed.
Comprehensive analysis reveals that PatchNet excels computationally and
architecturally in comparison to state-of-the-art models.

The discrete time asymmetric simple exclusion process (TASEP) exhibits an intriguing property where its multi-point distribution is completely determined by its initial conditions. While the mathematical proof of this phenomenon is well-established, a comprehensive analytical representation of the multi-point distribution is lacking, particularly for cases involving non-biased initial configurations. To address this gap, a new approach is presented in which the Kuperberg-Kingi model is utilized. By applying this method, the asymptotic multi-point distribution is successfully evaluated for various initial bitstrings, a finding that broadens the understanding of TASEP's behavior under a wide range of initial conditions.

This study introduces an improved antenna-switching method to maximize the energy efficiency of networks that integrate simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT). We develop a Generalized Antenna-Switching Technique (GAST) which involves selecting the optimal number of antennas and assigning them to SWIPT networks. Our findings show that GAST enhances the reliability and data rates while minimizing the required transmission power. Building upon this concept, we formulate and solve the energy efficiency problem in SWIPT networks by jointly optimizing these factors. Due to the intricate nature of the problem, we propose an alternating optimization method that alternates between determining the best antennas and power allocation. Furthermore, we introduce the Gaussian Mixing Property to ensure the feasibility of solutions. Our results demonstrate that GAST offers a comprehensive and efficient approach to address the challenges in SWIPT networks.

We present a detailed analytical approach to first-order perturbations in SU(N) fermion models. Our method employs the Feynman-Schwinger representation, incorporating an integral over Lorentz vectors. This perturbation theory yields the second-order correction to the fermion propagator, which we verify against existing theories. For a general SU(N) gauge group, our results suggest that the second-order correction deviates from analytical predictions by a factor of N, or more accurately $N-1$, in the large-N limit. We also examine the impact of the Lorentz factor on this discrepancy. By introducing a new integral over Lorentz vectors in the perturbative framework, we find that choosing Landau gauge ($\lambda = 0$)$ eliminates the discrepancy. For SU(2) and SU(3) gauge groups, the Lorentz factor's effect is minimal, with differences less than 5% and 2% respectively. However, in the large-N limit, perturbative corrections fail to account for the discrepancy between analytical and lattice results.

The interaction between light and mechanical elements is a key component in optomechanics, and it is useful to understand how classical electrical circuit models compare with quantum treatments when the number of quanta is high. We explore this issue through various circuit configurations and find that, in certain scenarios with large occupation numbers, the electrical circuit models accurately reflect the quantum treatments of light and sound interactions. However, there are notable discrepancies between the two models, such as the lack of phase damping in the classical approach, and issues with assuming continuous modes of sound for electrical resonators. We highlight situations where classical and quantum descriptions diverge and suggest experimental tests to verify these differences.

The orthogonal polynomials of the generalized Freud type, denoted as $P_n$, for n=0 to infinity, with respect to the generalized Freud weight $w_{\lambda,\mu}(x)$ in the real domain, have been determined to be equivalent to the Laguerre-Hermite polynomials $L_n^{(\lambda)}(x^2)$ when $\mu$ equals 1. Furthermore, two key properties of the generalised Freud polynomials have been identified, namely a recurrence relation and a differential equation. To verify the validity of these polynomials, their Christoffel-Darboux formula has been proven and used to generate the corresponding generalised Freud coefficients for x^k. The moments for $P_n(x)$ have been determined and their validity has been confirmed through the application of the recurrence relation and the previously proven relation. As a special case, the generalised Airy weight $e^{-|x|^{\lambda}/2}$ is obtained when $\mu$ equals -1. The generalised Freud coefficients for $P_n(x)$ have been found to be the same as those for the Legendre polynomials when $\lambda$ equals 0 and $\mu$ equals -1. The generalised sextic Freud weight differs from the generalised Airy weight by a multiplicative constant.

This research examines the influence of the field of view (FoV) of a distance sensor on the movement and path of a follow-the-wall robot, taking into consideration its working distance. By employing a two-dimensional Markov chain model, we analyze how the sensor's sampling frequency, detection range, and other factors impact the robot's trajectory. The study reveals that the robot's movement and path are sensitive to the FoV, ranging, and sampling frequency of the sensor used, highlighting the significance of sensor selection in robot design. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between these parameters and the characteristics of the robot's trajectory, providing insight into the blending effect of discrete sensor readings on robot movement.

In the framework of perturbative algebraistic quantum field theory, subalgebras of the global perturbative algebra are defined on specific Cauchy surfaces, which influence the associated subalgebras even when these surfaces do not extend to infinity.  This phenomenon raises the question of how to isolate subalgebras that depend on specific Cauchy surfaces, an issue also present in perturbative classical field theory.  We investigate the Cauchy surface dependent factor algebras for perturbative classical and quantum free scalar field theories.  By analyzing the factor algebras, differences in definitions are identified and implications discussed, one definition (factor algebras) is shown to lead to non-local observables influenced by distant regions, which is inconsistent with the expected behavior in perturbative algebraic quantum field theory.

Smoke detection during surgical procedures is a challenging task, particularly as smoke images can appear very similar. To address this issue, we have developed a novel neural network-based approach that utilizes training data generated through a smoke simulator to enhance smoke and non-smoke image classification. Our technique employs a BERT model for image representation and pre-training, leveraging the semantic connections between images and text to improve accuracy. The effectiveness of this approach has been validated by our experimental results, which indicate a higher rate of correct smoke and non-smoke image predictions.

A new approach to creating robust gates for the Molmer-Sorensen technique is developed, particularly for use in small-scale ion chains. Due to fluctuations in key variables, the effectiveness of existing MS gates is limited to chains of no more than 10 ions. In an effort to improve their reliability, these frequency-resilient gates combine multiple frequency components, each meticulously controlled using a simple linear model, to compensate for individual gate deviations. Through simulations, the researchers demonstrate the ability to maintain entanglement growth across up to 200 ions, double the previous limit of 10, as well as preserve the quantum correlations within 20-ion chains, far exceeding the 10-ion threshold. Additionally, the researchers examine how errors in modeling affect these gates and analyze the efficiency trade-off between the number of control parameters used and the resulting entanglement generation. In an attempt to optimize the gate's performance, the researchers incorporate both short-term and long-term Hamiltonian interactions into the gate, yielding enhanced resilience.

Non-centrosymmetric behavior in perovskites has been observed in certain materials despite lacking the necessary conditions for proper ferroelectricity. Using first-principles calculations, researchers investigated the origins of off-centering behavior in both equilibrium and non-stoichiometric scenarios for A-site deficient perovskites. They focused on three cations at the B-site with varying sizes and one type of non-stoichiometric scenario for a specific material. Equilibrium volume and the presence of larger A-site cations were found to significantly influence off-centering behavior. In particular, they revealed a sizeable A-site cation effect, where off-centerings were found to be suppressed when larger cations occupied non-stoichiometric sites. These findings were consistent with experimental observations and could potentially guide the search for new materials exhibiting proper ferroelectricity.

We introduce ConGP, a system that allows the creation of large-scale graphical models by combining multiple Gaussian processes, each representing a distinct variable over its own set of nodes in the graph. The system ensures that the structure of the graph accurately reflects the conditional independence of its functions. By using a shared set of hyperparameters and a common likelihood function across multiple univariate GPs, ConGP promotes consistency among its nodes and can effectively manage resources when split among multiple processors. We use a Hamiltonian Monte Carlo algorithm to optimize the shared hyperparameters and local variables of each GP, which we have tested in a workflow that involves predicting the outcomes of 222 financial decisions made by companies.

We examine the capacity of quantum circuits with repeating structures to efficiently obtain the ground state energies and wavefunctions of hydrogen and hydrogen-like ion systems. Using the variable-angle variational quantum phase estimation algorithm, our study shows that even with limited pattern depth, ground state calculations can be accurately achieved. We utilize these results as a foundation for further investigation into recurrent quantum circuits' potential in more intricate algorithms for achieving more expensive computations efficiently.

We introduce the Generalized Chebyshev method, a family of optimization algorithms capable ofGCertifying average-case performance superior to that of classical optimization algorithms, such as gradient descent, on various problems. This method includes as a special case the new Generalized Newton method. Unlike the original Newton's method, which already exhibits such performance on strongly convex functions, the Generalized Newton method exhibits even better performance. Furthermore, it can achieve this advantage while being applied to a broader range of functions than the original Newton's method.

Moiré superlattices exhibit a unique property, where the presence of an electric field enables the manipulation of their moiré period and leads to the formation of a sea of interlayer excitons. In this work, theoretical density functional calculations are performed to study the electronic and optical behavior of moiré structures and their excitation energies in monolayer and bilayer graphene, as well in other materials such as transition metal dichalcogenides. Computational results indicate that the presence of an electric field causes the conduction band to cross the Fermi level enabling the formation of a large number of interlayer excitons which significantly affect the optical spectra and result in a redshift. Moreover, the energy of the interlayer excitons is found to be influenced by their density and the range of the Coulomb interaction. Specifically, the presence of interlayer excitons causes a decrease in the energy of the lowest energy interlayer excitons in moiré graphene, a phenomenon which is attributed to the repulsive Coulomb interaction between them.

We develop an efficient, robust algorithm for accurately tracking a moving object in real-time under diverse and changing observational conditions. The algorithm incorporates a cutting-edge feature: a sophisticated data association method that utilizes probabilistic analysis and a sophisticated data filtering technique modeled after the Kalman-Bucy algorithm. To further improve performance, we integrate a sophisticated gridding system that adaptively focuses on the most relevant areas, thereby enhancing the algorithm's ability to handle outliers effectively.

The LHCb experiment, analyzing 90 fb^-1 of data collected at 13 TeV from proton-proton collisions, presents an examination of the production of WW, WZ, and WWZW systems in a study of the bb bar system's dijet mass above 600 GeV. In a study of over 300,000 WW, WZ, and ZZ events, the vector boson polarization configurations are analyzed using advanced techniques. A study of over 100,000 events reveals the joint helicity fractions of W and Z bosons, and these findings are in line with the Standard Model predictions. Moreover, the transverse momentum of the decay leptons from WW, WZ, and ZZ events is also examined, and the results are used to derive upper limits on the production of heavy new resonances decaying to lepton-plus-neutrino or lepton-lepton pairs, enabling the exploration of new physics within the LHC's operational parameters.

We develop a Causal Set Theory that incorporates stress-energy, achieving this goal by establishing how a discrete theory's vacuum state Cottos tensor corresponds to a zero value, and then establishing a quantitative relationship between this tensor and the stress-energy tensor at a point. Our approach involves redefining the concept of a point as a hyper-volume and a surface as an element in the element in the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the element of the

A non-commutative structure called an orthomodular space has been proposed to model various phenomena observed in quantum physics and set theory. Researchers have found that certain operations on the ortholattice of open sets of a topological space create a equivalence with another mathematical model known as an orthomodular poset, specifically through the inclusion of pseudo-complement operations and topological properties. This equivalence allows for a unified approach to interpreting abstract orthomodular lattices by embedding them into the orthomodular spaces. The method involves the use of a topological structure to represent the poset, providing a new perspective on quantum physics and set theory.

Researchers have developed innovative techniques to create meaningful, 
graphical descriptions of the reasoning processes behind solutions to 
complex problems and to automatically generate the solutions themselves. 
These techniques have significant applications in automated theorem 
proving and the automated solution of algebraic equations. 
We explore how the generated proof representations can be employed to 
streamline the review process and enhance the reliability of the 
auto-generated solutions, as well as how the underlying technologies can 
be applied to other tasks, such as generating the proofs from the 
established truths. 
Additionally, we highlight the value of these technologies in the 
development of automated learning systems capable of providing well- 
structured, understandable, and detailed explanations for tasks like the 
identification of objects and the understanding of the content in written 
texts.

We break down the first moment in a specific range given by Watson's formulation for the product of adjacent $L$-functions. To do this, we leverage his formula along with earlier progress on a related problem within the Sato-Tate framework, as well as as a consequence of our research, which also provides new insights into the second moment.

Interior point methods are a widely used class of algorithms that can be applied to various optimization problems, including those in compressed sensing.  Initial research found that interior point methods were efficient at determining if a compressed sensing problem could be solved, although some of these algorithms had extremely long running times.  More recent work has revealed that interior point methods are actually efficient at solving large compressed sensing problems, but only if the inner iterations are terminated earlier than previously thought necessary.  The main goal of the paper is to provide a clear explanation for the success of interior point methods in the context of compressed sensing problems.

Recently, a new 3-flavor number scheme has been suggested to resolve a long-standing issue with determining the strong interaction coupling constant from a specific benchmark measurement. This problem arises due to the conflict between the predicted value based on all-order perturbative calculations and the observed value in a ring-shaped ring-gauge experiment. This conflict only occurs in the variable flavor number scheme, which varies the number of flavor. Therefore, a transition function that manages the change from a 4-flavor to a 3-flavor number scheme is necessary. This paper develops such a transition function, specifically $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$, and provides its explicit form for $N=3$. Additionally, the paper discusses the relationship between this newly developed function and previously established transition schemes, including those from massive-dimension-regularization and fixed 3-flavor number schemes.

We have compiled a comprehensive AI Incident Database, which serves as a knowledge base to facilitate learning and advancement in AI. This database contains a vast collection of AI-related incidents, drawing from diverse AI research disciplines, and spans a wide range of topics from inciting questions and highlighted promising paths. Our database is freely accessible online at https://ai-incidents.org and aims to inspire the AI community to create, innovate, and contribute more incident reports. The collection currently encompasses 154 documented AI incidents, which can be explored here: https://ai-incidents.org.

A specific relative entropy generalization differential equation for Yang-Mills theory has been successfully developed. In tandem with the BFH flow, this ERG equation ensures the BF flow's infrared fixed point is maintained within the Yang-Mills theory framework, thereby maintaining gauge invariance. Notably, this approach aligns the BF flow's fixed point with a known solvable model, the topological theory. The created framework facilitates an investigation into potential differences in BF flow initial conditions for pure Yang-Mills theory and QCD. By leveraging this framework, a direct comparison of the pure Yang-Mills and QCD flows becomes possible, enabling an in-depth exploration of the role of quarks in the flow dynamics. Furthermore, this approach allows for an examination of the flow's sensitivity to initial conditions and the flow's impact on the flow's result.

A business process monitoring system compares actual process data to established specifications and flags any deviations. When multiple rules conflict, however, providing useful insights becomes challenging. This study presents a novel approach that leverages a labeling system and predictive analysis to flag and explain deviations from specification and predict future process outcomes. By assigning labels to instances based on their behavior, the system can offer a more accurate understanding of what to expect next and identify which parts of the specification are violated. Our system assigns a 'high-risk' label to instances that breach a high-priority specification and predicts a high probability of future problems, enabling users to receive more precise and context-aware monitoring.

This text presents a formal system, Proto-Quipper-M, built upon a logical foundation that keeps the properties of quantum mechanics intact, particularly the rule that quantum states cannot be copied. By treating classical and quantum circuits as structures within this system and applying a translating function to convert them into specified logical forms, we demonstrate that the system's non-cloning property is maintained. This approach is consistent with previously established work and serves as a starting point for developing an interactive tool to verify quantum circuits and their properties.

Using the eigenvalues of a specific type of random-matrix model, we have developed a numerical framework for studying critical phenomena and self-similar patterns in one-dimensional quantum systems. By applying finite-size scaling to these eigenvalues, we can accurately characterize continuous quantum phase transitions. Our approach leverages the precise, computationally efficient calculation of a specific type of matrix determinant, and utilizes an analytically continuous extension of this calculation. This enables us to efficiently obtain the entire spectrum of one-class random-matrix models, which have become increasingly relevant in various areas of quantum physics. Our study incorporates the one-dimensional Heisenberg ferromagnet and a specific boundary-interaction model as test cases.

Two-mode squeezing can be employed to improve the precision of quantum-enhanced optical phase sensing, but it's necessary to compensate for the effects of a phase shift on this precision. Our research presents an innovative approach for post-processing experimental data to mitigate these compensation effects. Unlike conventional methods, which only measure the mean value, our technique also takes advantage of the reduced variance in experimental measurements to develop an optimal estimator for the phase parameter. The improved accuracy achieved enables a more effective management of uncertainties when estimating a quantum state parameter. The refined estimator can be applied to a broad range of quantum states, including those used in optical clocks and optical coherence tomography in their most sensitive configurations.

As genomic sequences grow in size, the need for efficient ways to divide huge datasets has become critical. We have created a new method called multiway number partitioning that evenly distributes an increasing number of genomic sequences across multiple processors. This approach enables the simultaneous splitting of k sequences across p processors, with our algorithm guaranteeing a maximum difference of three in the number of edges between any two subsets. By integrating this algorithm with existing multiway number partitioning software, we have shown that it significantly speeds up the assembly of increasingly larger genomes on supercomputers.

A proposed modification to the logistic equation for delayed cell population growth is presented. This new model incorporates a growth rate that varies over time based on the cell population's past, divided by the time since those cells' population was measured and the cell population at that point. It is demonstrated through various approaches that this equation has a stable, positive equilibrium for any positive initial condition. Furthermore, a boundary value problem formulation is developed, along with existence and uniqueness solutions using a constructive method. This new approach to delayed cell growth offers advantages in model parameter estimation from real data due to the availability of a well-defined, unique parameter initial value problem.

A point process, describing the Isometric Log-Ratio (ILR)-transformed interarrival times of a homogeneous Poisson process from different time scales, has been developed. These Isometric Log-Ratio (ILR) transformations convert compositional data, resolving issues stemming from the bounded simple sum constraint. They also address problems related to unevenly measured event times. The transformation preserves geometric structures, facilitating statistical analysis in an orthogonal coordinate system. The paper derives the stochastic properties of the transformed vector and compares it to the raw interarrival times, along with a case study illustrating its benefits.

The properties of hybrid quantum conductors, which include quantum electrodynamic effects and entangled Cooper pair behavior, make them valuable for generating and processing quantum information and designing novel devices.
