The ability to control these effects however remains limited by their interdependence with the device's physical structure. A new class of devices has been developed to independently control these effects and design complex entanglement circuits. Specifically, a hybrid quantum circuit has been designed to separate and control these effects in closely connected superconductor-semiconductor nanowire junctions. The successful operation of the circuit, involving the localization of entangled Cooper pairs and the conversion of their charge into detectable voltage, has also been demonstrated. Its development provides a framework for the study of quantum information and novel quantum devices based on hybrid quantum systems.

Investigations into the intricate relationship between nuclear structure and nuclear mass have been a central theme in the study of mass formulas. This paper examines four distinct nonlinear relationships between moments of inertia and nuclear structures for even-even nuclei in nickel, germanium, strontium, and zirconium, exploring how nuclear mass changes affect their rotational properties. A notable shift in nuclear structure is observed from nickel to germanium around neutron number 40, resulting in nickel exhibiting a soft spherical shape, whereas germanium displays a rigid intermediate oblate deformation. This shift marks a transition from nickel's soft spherical symmetry to a more rigid intermediate oblate shape in germanium. Conversely, the transition from strontium to zirconium around neutron number 64 exhibits a point of maximum softness in nuclear mass, exhibiting a smooth change from a prolate oblate shape in strontium to a more rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded rounded

The production cross sections for a variety of short-lived neutron-deficient nuclides, specifically $^{103}_{54}$Mo, $^{103}_{53}$I, $^{104}_{53}$I, $^{106}_{53}$I, $^{107}_{53}$I, $^{112}_{54}$Xe, $^{113}_{54}$Xe, and $^{114}_{54}$Xe, were experimentally measured for the first time using the GANIL $\\beta$-$\\rho$-Ion Source Material Source Beamline (GISMO) and a high-resolution time-of-flight mass spectrometer (RTOFMR). The experiments were conducted with thick natural target stations and in particular targeted the production of very short-lived Mo, I, and Xe isotopes via projectile fragmentation using $^{136}$Xe and $^{132}$Sn beams. The GISMO beamline played a key role in overcoming a series of bottlenecks that had previously hindered the development of new methods for producing and analysing very short-lived isotopes. The experimental cross-sectional measurements were compared with theoretical predictions made using the TALYS code, which yielded a satisfactory match.

Machine learning models that achieve gauge invariance from the start are essential for developing reliable and accurate U(1) gauge theories. Currently, there is a lack of neural network-based models that are both gauge invariant and normalizing flow models, which are crucial for sampling and simulation. In this work, we introduce a novel method to create gauge-invariant normalizing flows, applying it to the abelian lattice gauge theory. The framework involves starting with an arbitrary neural network and applying two additional layers: one approximates the SU(2) group action, and the other approximates a permutation matrix. The result is a normalizing flow model for Q-Lattice gauge theory. The efficiency and effectiveness of this model are demonstrated through sampling and simulation of the abelian lattice gauge theory. The approach may also be applicable to lattice gauge theories with other groups and continuum quantum field theories that involve symmetries.

This research focuses on the potential for bias to be leveraged in task-specific language models, focusing on the ability to identify text formatted in a particular way, such as phone numbers or emails. It demonstrates that models biased towards a correct answer can achieve higher accuracy, and that this bias does not necessarily negatively impact the model's performance on other tasks. Various bias induction and evaluation methods are presented, along with a proposed framework for assessing bias without compromising the model's utility in various applications.

This report presents an overview of production techniques and properties of top quarks, based on production measurements, and compares these to predictions from perturbative quantum chromodynamics (QCD). Furthermore, it offers a summary of the top quark's theoretical mass calculation within the framework of perturbative QCD.

Execution accuracy is heavily dependent on in-flight data, which is unpredictable and difficult to model. A new execution accuracy prediction framework addresses this challenge by decoupling execution accuracy from in-flight data. The framework consists of two key components: (1) an in-flight data-independent predictor that calculates a normalized prediction value based on outcome sequences, regardless of the in-flight data; and (2) an adaptive adjustment mechanism that takes account of any discrepancies between predicted and actual outcomes. The proposed framework outperforms current best approaches in TPC-C and TASB benchmarks, with in-flight data sensitivity and CDB miss sensitivity also showing comparable performance to state-of-the-art alternatives. The code for our method has been made available on GitHub.

We analyze the Low Frequency Array Sky Survey (LoTSS) galaxy catalog containing 13,443 galaxies with redshifts exceeding 0.1, to investigate the predicted characteristics of angular clustering as a function of redshift under the $\Lambda$CDM cosmological model. Comparing observed and simulation-based estimates of the power spectrum $w(r_0)$ for three distinct redshift bins reveals discrepancies at the $1\sigma$ to $2.5\sigma$ level. These discrepancies are attributed to a lower observed galaxy density in our sample and variations in angular diameter distance in the $\Lambda$CDM model. Despite these findings, we observe no evidence of tension with angular diameter distance predictions within $\Lambda$CDM. Furthermore, we find that LoTSS measurements of the power spectrum align closely with previous observations from the Dark Energy Survey's Baryon Acoustic Oscillation tomography, and we project that future LoTSS releases may yield estimates of $w(r_0)$ at the $1\sigma$ level, potentially enabling a precise empirical probe of angular diameter distance while remaining sensitive to galaxy bias non-linearities.

The `rasso` problem with high dimensional rank constraints often involves sparse and large-scale data sets, making its efficient computation a pressing issue. A proposed algorithm, based on adaptive sieving methods, addresses this challenge by effectively handling the sparsity of rasso's optimal solution. Drawing from the success of similar approaches in l0-regularized optimization problems, this algorithm iteratively refines its solution set and solves subproblems along the non-zero support set. Furthermore, it proposes a novel initial strategy to enhance its convergence speed. Through thorough numerical experiments on both l0-regularized and l2-regularized (rasso) optimization problems, the algorithm demonstrates a significant reduction in compute time, showcasing its practical value for real-world data analysis.

Building on previous findings about the non-uniqueness of stationary states with minimal entropy production rate in certain quantum systems, this work demonstrates that there is a unique global optimal protocol for quantum systems that come into contact with two heat baths at distinct temperatures, if the protocol's entropy production rate is strictly convex in its initial state. Furthermore, this uniqueness surpasses existing results by applying to both quantum and quantum thermodynamic systems. The proof utilizes a generalized quantum version of the Stochastic Max-Planck distribution. As a consequence, there is a unique optimal protocol that minimizes the total work needed to achieve a target state in global quantum thermodynamic optimization problems.

There's been significant discussion about the environmental impact of AI services, yet there's a lack of concrete methods to quantify this footprint in practice. To address this gap, we employ life cycle assessment (LCA) to evaluate the energy consumption of AI services running on different hardware configurations. We use (location, energy mix, and) virtual machine (L-E-M-V) footprints to measure the dynamic scaling of workloads across varying infrastructure settings. By applying this approach to four machine learning (L-E-M-V) footprints, we employ simple and hybrid LCAs to compare the carbon footprints of two image classification models, MobileNetV2 and ResNet50, across a range of physical hardware scenarios. The study reveals that the choice of machine learning model often has a more significant impact on carbon emissions than the type of hardware it runs on, and our approach offers a more comprehensive understanding of the dynamic energy footprint of AI services, contributing to the development of more carbon-efficient AI services.

Prescriptive process monitoring method development relies heavily on the assumption that historical data reflects the same conditions under which these methods will be applied in practice. To address this assumption, a novel data-driven approach is proposed to evaluate the predictive performance of OPM methods under real-world circumstances, where an organization's response to previously unforeseen events may deviate from past patterns. This approach evaluates the generalizability of recommended actions by comparing the observed post-alarm behavior to the low-confidence reference data, without requiring access to post-alarm data. By measuring behavior similarity using a post-alarm distance metric, the approach reveals the performance limitations and underlying assumptions of OPM methods, thereby facilitating the development of more reliable and effective recommendations. Through case studies of the T2S algorithm, the effectiveness of the proposed evaluation method, the value of early warning data, and the T2S algorithm's ability to generalize its recommendations are illustrated.

To solve the coupled problem of Darcy-forced natural convection, we employ the continuous and discrete dual-weighted residual method for error estimation, which also functions as adaptive refinement guidance. This approach involves using the solution of the continuous problem in the discrete dual problem. Furthermore, the method is applied within a local, residual-based a posteriori error estimator framework, which is founded on the concept that the test functions in the dual problem mimic the solution's gradient in the primal problem. We utilize the method to develop an error estimator for the coupled problem and conduct numerical experiments to verify its effectiveness.

The main objective of the graph packing problem is to determine the largest subgraphs within a given graph that collectively form multiple copies of a specified target graph in a vertex- and edge-disjoint manner. In particular, finding the maximum number of disjoint paths within a graph represents a fundamental graph packing task. However, directly computing tight bounds for this problem remains a challenging objective. In this study, we introduce a new approach based on the linear relaxation of a conventional integer programming formulation to establish upper limits for the maximum number of disjoint paths. By integrating this bound with existing techniques, such as those found in [K. D. Clough, D. W. Matula, D. S. Rall, Dynamic lower bounds for the path packing problem, Discrete Applied Mathematics, 2017], we successfully calculate maximum numbers of disjoint paths of length 4 in various graphs.

This work explores the one-dimensional dynamics of opinion formation where to adopt a more nuanced approach, we consider opinions not as fixed entities but as evolving continuously. One-dimensional opinions naturally lead to the emergence of distinct social cliques, yet existing models often fail to capture the evolution of these groups. To bridge this gap, a new model is proposed that facilitates the formation and temporal evolution of cliques, along with an analysis of the model's statistical properties in both single and multi-clique scenarios. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that our model can be parametrically tuned to mimic real-world social and financial complex networks.

We investigate a previously little-explored phenomenon, where a global symmetry, present in the dual theory, results in a distinct type of hair on a black hole. This is achieved through the utilization of a scalar field with an intricate, globally symmetric underlying structure. By employing a holographic superconductor as a concrete example, we demonstrate how the model's dual theory, featuring a global U(1) symmetry, can still produce a black hole with global U(1) type of hair. This is made possible by using a quaternionic scalar field. Moreover, we explore the connection between this novel type of hair and the oscillating modes associated with the phase transition in the dual theory.

Our model provides a theoretical framework for understanding gene dynamics, focusing on the delay between transcription and the production of mature mRNA. For this purpose, we have developed an abstract model of a gene, which can be extended to include multiple genes and gene clusters. This expanded model preserves the essential features of a single gene while allowing for more complex genomic arrangements. In the case of genes located at the end of a chromosome, our model predicts that the production of mature mRNA is not accurately represented by traditional stochastic chemical mass action models, as the gene length plays a significant role in the transcription process. For genes located in the middle of a chromosome, our model shows that the probability distribution of the transcription time is the same, but the distribution of the translation time is affected by the gene length. To address these complexities, we have developed a new stochastic model that incorporates the effects of gene length on transcription and translation processes. For the most part, this stochastic model matches the probability distributions of the extended gene model, with one exception: the probability distribution of the total protein production is affected by the gene length even when the transcription and translation rates are independent of the gene length. To address this issue, we have developed an adjusted chemical mass action model that accounts for the effects of gene length on protein production. This model is applicable to any gene location and can be used to predict the effects of gene length on protein production. Our model provides a more accurate representation of gene dynamics than traditional stochastic chemical mass action models, which do not

High-energy excitation data for the nucleus $^{64}$Ni has been re-evaluated using Monte Carlo Shell Model calculations to examine the changes in neutron subshell gaps and monopole interaction as neutrons are added to the $^{58}$Ni core. A shell structure analysis of the $^{58-70}$Ni isotopes revealed that our results are in line with the experimentally observed trends in neutron subshell gaps and monopole interaction softness. Notably, these findings help to understand how the excitation energy evolves in the $^{64}$Ni nucleus up to high excitation energies, offering a local explanation for the large drop from $$B(E2;6^- \to 0_1^\+)^{58}Ni$$ to $$B(E2;6^- \to 0_1^\+)^{64}Ni$$ values.

The 2020 review by Beane and Bedaque on low-energy heavy baryon standard model effective field theory (HB\SMEFT) will be supplemented with recent advancements made in our understanding heavy baryon effective field theory and the formulation of the standard model effective field theory.

A linear code is defined as D^perp, where D^perp is equivalent to a group code C. 
Established definitions and the inherent connections between C and D, including C's dual, 
are explored. Additional properties and relationships are also examined. 
Specifically, it's shown that C is equivalent to a group code derived from its dual. 
Two group codes are identified as duals to each other, resulting in the code D^perp being self-dual when applied to C. 
Consequently, it's proven that a group code is self-dual if and only if its dual code is self-dual. 
It's additionally shown that a group code from an abelian group generates a self-dual code if specific conditions are met. 
The code D^perp, defined from group codes over Z_2 and Z_3 groups, is identified as a code that can form a self-dual code if and only if it meets a length criterion. 
The code D^perp, defined from codes over nonabelian groups, also exists and relationships are explored. 
It's shown that a group code from a nonabelian group cannot be self-dual. 
Finally, it's established that a group code from a nonabelian group cannot generate a self-dual code.

Our developed algorithm, Bucket Elimination, takes advantage of the structure in a model to efficiently perform various optimization and inference computations on undirected and directed models, as well as unbounded arithmetic circuits. When used for optimization tasks, we obtain a simplified objective, and for inference, we obtain a more simplified circuit. These computations are facilitated by our approach, yielding efficient running times under certain conditions. Furthermore, we have extended BE to enable efficient rejection sampling, obtaining a sample complexity of O~(exp tilde{m})) where {m} represents the smallest width in the elimination order of the circuit's variables. Our developed algorithms exhibit improved efficiency over existing methods in specific instances, and our rejection sampling algorithm outperforms the best alternative by an exponential margin in some cases.

Our goal is to train a multi-sensory system, using visual and auditory input, to identify both normal and anomalous events of a falling object, even when the drop deviates from typical parameters. To achieve this, we leverage self-supervised learning to train separate visual and auditory models, which help us incorporate domain-specific knowledge of the object's flight path, air resistance, and other physical principles. This integrated information is used to guide the fusion of the two models for normal and anomalous drop classification. As part of our study, we've compiled a novel, open dataset comprising both data from a visible fall and compressed audio of nine different object types.

Continuing our investigation into the universality of isotropic jamming phases and transitions, we now focus on shear jamming under friction. Through computer simulations of the astatic isotropic continuous shear transformation zone model, we find a distinct jamming transition when a constant shear strain is applied and identify its properties via finite-size scaling analysis. Not only do scaling exponents and the Jamming Point differ between isotropic and shear jamming transitions, but their frictionless counterparts also exhibit unique characteristics and are thus unlikely to serve as a effective reduced description for the more intricate friction present in shear jamming.

This study develops the MS(2)-AR(4) model to model electricity demand, which exhibits distinct behaviors in two distinct regimes, combined with an underlying stochastic process. Each regime has its distinct AR(4) properties, enabling the model to accommodate multiple variance levels and non-stationary characteristics. Leveraging the model's closed form solution and the characteristics of the multivariate t-distribution derived from a mixture of Gaussian distributions, the paper proposes an alternative maximum likelihood estimation method to capture the complex dynamics of electricity demand. Comparative analysis reveals that the MS(2)-AR(4) model outperforms the traditional autoregressive model in accurately capturing electricity demand dynamics and provides more accurate point forecasts for a single regulator than an autoregressive model, particularly during the transition periods between regimes.

Several studies have highlighted growing concerns about biases in computer systems, particularly among professionals working within the public sector. This knowledge gap is crucial for policymakers, educators, and professionals to address the pervasive biases in algorithmic Web search results. This study builds on prior research by examining how search engine results for "algorithmic bias" are biased among search professionals, particularly those working in public sector organizations. A total of 289 participants were asked to perform Google searches and rate the resulting pages on a bias scale. The most common searches were analyzed by a group of 36 search professionals, including educators, policymakers, and researchers, who evaluated the pages similarly. The majority of participants and a substantial number of search professionals agreed on the presence of bias in search results. However, when measuring degree bias, the results showed that educators and search professionals agreed more frequently on a moderate level of bias, while policymakers and researchers agreed more frequently on a high level of bias. The implications and broader relevance of these findings are discussed in relation to various groups.

Our research focuses on developing an innovative, user-centered synthesis system that enables non-expert users to create the right program by specifying what it should do, rather than how to do it. Traditional synthesis frameworks are too complex and restrictive for these users to understand, so we developed a novel approach. By integrating the framework into the user's editor and analyzing their input, the system automatically synthesizes a program that matches the user's specification. This approach is particularly effective for programs that involve basic data manipulations like sorting and filtering. As a result, users can quickly and efficiently communicate their intentions, allowing our framework to quickly synthesize the desired program, even handling multiple variables and operations. The framework successfully synthesizes a program 90% of the time within less than three seconds, and our users rate the synthesized program 80% of the time as exactly what they intended. The framework is easy to implement in any text editor with minimal additional code.

We've examined how different reduction methods can aid in clumping together the climate system's complex dynamics and explored their effect on the climate's various biosphere-physico-chemical models. This research involved a detailed analysis of the processes involved in reducing complex climate models. Such climate models are typically built using a combination of diverse software, resulting in challenges in identifying and simplifying their underlying dynamics. Reduction methods serve as a valuable tool to group related climate system components and have been extensively used in the CLM-CM5 model's development. This study examined the climate model's behavior both in its original form and after using three reduction methods: Krylov, Schur, and KL methods. The results from each method were compared to assess their impact on the model's reduction. The finding suggested that while all three methods contributed to understanding the climate's complex dynamics, the KL method was the most effective in preserving the model's output and was subsequently used to develop reduced-order models (ROMs) for ClM-CM5. The research also involved using ROMs to rapidly assess the climate's response to baseline and perturbed boundary conditions. The find demonstrated that the reduced models were able to maintain the accuracy of the full-order model (FOM) while providing significant computational savings. The subsequent step is to further validate the reduced models by comparing their predictions to the original model's results to establish their reliability for use in model emulation and other climate-related applications.

Gravitational wave events that also involve matter ejections can lead to the creation of opacities in the kilonova, which absorb and scatter light at specific wavelengths in the infrared spectrum. The James Webb Space Telescope's sensitivity in fine-structure lines, particularly at 10.53 micrometers, can be leveraged to study the broad absorption features caused by these events. This feature is predicted to be visible in the upcoming kilonova from the neutron star merger associated with the GW190814 gravitational wave, provided matter is transferred to the ejecta. The 10.53 micrometer fine-structure line is distinct from other absorption features and can be used as a diagnostic tool to study the matter transfer. Its observation would revolutionize the study of kilonovae, offering a new perspective on the complex processes involved in the mergers of compact compact objects.

When treating patients with X-ray beams, radiation oncologists face difficulties in accurately aligning the beams without clear visual cues for tumor and organ location. Real-time X-ray imaging can assist but comes with costs and safety risks due to increased staff exposure. Although automated tumor imaging exists, issues with image quality and speed remain. Our approach involves using deep learning and morphological analysis to estimate tumor shapes and positions from low-quality images, thereby improving the accuracy of subsequent X-ray system alignments.

In compositional data analysis, the lognormal model is a frequently used approach to represent high-dimensional data vectors by log-transforming their components, with parameters expressed as a multivariate normal distribution. Following log-transformation, the covariance matrix is often a considered parameter. In the ComCo approach to compositional data analysis, data vectors are first closed, with a common measure being the geometric closure. A recent study investigated the maximum likelihood estimation of multivariate normal distribution parameters based on geometric closure. Building on this, the current paper extends the investigation to the lognormal model parameters, specifically the covariance matrix, in the context of compositional data analysis.

The discovery of numerous exoplanets has enabled researchers to examine statistical trends among planetary systems. Researchers have mapped exoplanet distributions and found discrepancies between the predictions of the core accretion model - the leading theory for planetary formation - and the observed data, particularly regarding runaway gas accretion. This paper explores the potential solution to this discrepancy by considering the impact of accretion that occurs over time intervals from the end of the disc phase to the present. This approach is modeled using simplified equations and applied to examine key statistical trends. By doing so, the team found that accounting for delayed growth can make the core accretion model's predictions align more closely with the observed planetary distributions, including planetary mass and number distributions. Moreover, the model is shown to predict a specific power law for massive planetary candidates, which is in line with empirical evidence.

A novel work builds upon the existing Foundation Agents framework, enhancing it with a sophisticated, adaptive memory system and a deep recurrent network to accurately represent and analyze the agent's internal state. This memory architecture, composed of memory and gating units, automatically selects relevant memories and updates the agent's internal state, enabling it to track the client's unobserved states and refine predictions based on partial information. Furthermore, the FDMA architecture, comprising a memory module and a deep recurrent network, learns to represent the agent's internal state and analyze it, while the FDMA is trained using end-to-end gradient descent to maximize task-relevant predictions.

We examine non-resonant dark matter interactions with the nucleon through a scalar mediator, considering the mediator to be either spin-zero or spin-one-half. This interaction arises from integrating out the mediator at low energies, resulting in a scalar operator. The operator is then expressed as a linear combination of two scalar terms, which we analyze in detail. Our analysis reveals significant differences between the scattering properties of the mediator, depending on whether its mass is much lower or much higher than that of the dark matter. This leads to distinct features in the predicted nuclear recoil energy spectra for the mediator being lighter or heavier than the dark matter.

Existing collections of cognitive tasks are limited in terms of complexity,
variety, and number of tasks. To address these limitations, we propose a new
comprehensive set of cognitive tasks, named Mod-Cog, that offers greater
complexity, diversity, and multi-task learning capabilities. Our new battery
incorporates 24 tasks across 6 categories: memory, attention, learning,
processing speed, decision-making, and complex tasks, providing a more
thorough assessment of cognitive functions. We compare Mod-Cog to widely-used
sets of cognitive tasks and demonstrate that it effectively captures individual
differences, while also exploring the effects of multi-task learning and various
hardware environments. Mod-Cog is available for free at https://github.com/Mod-Cog/Mod-Cog.

We investigate the geometric structure of nilpotent algebra varieties. For any variety $\mathcal{V}$ of nilpotent $k$-algebras, where $k$ is a field, we establish that the points in this variety correspond to locally trivial families. We also show that functions within any variety $\mathcal{V}$ have the same dimension as the maximal subalgebra of the Jordan-Jacobsen classification. Additionally, we determine the function within the variety of irreducible nilpotent Jordan-Jacobsen algebras and calculate its dimension, where dimension is defined using function spaces. If $k$ is a finite field, $\mathcal{N}$, and $\mathcal{J}$ denote the sets of isomorphism classes of nilpotent Jordan-Jacobsen $k$-algebras, then we obtain lower and upper bounds for both sets.

The model suggests that the most prominent flat-spectrum radiation in large-scale jets originates from Inverse Compton scattering between high-speed electrons and the Cosmic Microwave Background, as opposed to the conventional view that the radio lobes emit radio synchrotron radiation and Inverse Compton scattering into higher frequencies. The theory predicts various characteristics that can be tested, such as the interaction of relativistic electrons with both the host's black hole jet and the interstellar medium. The model also takes into consideration how energy is transferred to relativistic electrons as they travel down the jet from the host's active core, as well as how energy is distributed among the jet components, all of which affect energy transfer and luminosity as observed. It is believed that this understanding will provide a more accurate framework for interpreting the observed energy distribution in large-scale jets and will lead to a more precise calculation of how these jets affect their surrounding environment, as opposed to the current model that may underestimate energy transfer and luminosity.

We compare two post-Newtonian and general relativity parametrizations to understand how they influence the analytical expandability of Schwarzschild coordinates in the PPN framework. The pre-non-relativistic approach, which defines velocity based on the Newtonian gravitational potential, allows post-Newtonian fields to be expressed as power series of this potential. In contrast, the pre-relativistic approach simplifies time in the PPN framework, while in general relativity, it corresponds to a specific metric. As a result, the pre-relativistic approach does not always permit an analytical expansion. We emphasize the significance of the power series format for expanding general relativity in the PPN framework. Moreover, we utilize the pre-non-relativistic parametrization to derive the pre-Newtonian Lagrangian, which is essential for deriving the pre-Newtonian equations of motion. These equations serve as a starting point for various applications, such as relic perturbation theory, where the pre-Newtonian background is used to study the growth of perturbations. We extend our research to include a new general relativity parametrization specifically designed for Schwarzschild coordinates, which we call the pre-non-relativistic PPN framework.

This research presents a novel method of image registration that combines Speeded Up Robust Features with compact support vector registration, specifically designed for the precise alignment of complex 3D medical volumetric images. The current methods of feature-based image registration often struggle in the context of medical imaging, particularly with changes in intensity contrast, local irregularities, or image quality. To address these challenges, we developed the SIFT-CPD method, which leverages the differences in image features and optimizes their geometric consistency. The SIFT-CPD approach utilizes Scale-Invariant Feature Transform to detect key points and variations in image intensities. To ensure a robust and geometrically consistent transformation, we employed the difference of compact convex projection divergence to estimate the change of motion. The effectiveness of the SIFT-CPD method was validated through experiments on magnetic resonance and computed tomography datasets for transrectal prostate biopsies, demonstrating a registration mean target deviation of as low as 2.9 mm for motion compensation data and a device trajectory deviation of 3.5 mm for distortion correction data. The source code for the SIFT-CPD method is publicly available at https://github.com/ProBioMed/SIFT-CPD.

We present an analysis of the properties of the detached binary system,
which consists of two white dwarf stars and exhibits variable eclipses in its light curve produced by the irregular shapes of its components.
Utilizing data from multiple sources, including photometry from the Zwicky Transient Facility and the X-ray archive of the same name, we have determined the dimensions and configurations of the system.
The analysis of its light curve reveals a particular configuration of its components and their respective sizes, while the analysis of its Zwicky photometry has enabled the calculation of their mass.
The findings suggest that the components of the binary system have masses of nearly equal value, and their sizes are comparable to those in the binary system GD 358, another variable star.
The coincidence of their masses places the binary within the instability strip of the Chandrasekhar limit, and its coexistence with the components of the binary in the X-ray transient class may suggest an interesting connection between the two phenomena.

A key concept in optimizing transport has emerged, particularly in the UOT (entropic optimal transport)-Pooling framework for neural networks. Notably, UOT-Pooling outperforms traditional average pooling in various benchmarks, such as image classification and semantic segmentation. Despite its potential, a limiting factor in adopting this framework is the computational cost associated with solving UOT dual variables. In response, we have developed a universal dual initialization technique for sUOT, enabling the efficient batch processing of multiple sUOT problems with differing cost matrices. By leveraging this technique, we have successfully incorporated it into the UOT-Pooling framework, specifically for image classification and semantic segmentation tasks. Our approach significantly enhances computational efficiency while maintaining the performance gains associated with UOT-Pooling.

The majority of the Theophanous et al. (2019) dataset consists of spiral host galaxies for NGC and ESO surveys, featuring naked or obscured nucleus of the galaxies. This study analyzes the morphological characteristics of these spiral hosts, as well as the shape of the galaxy's disk, the nucleus' position and shape, the distribution of the galaxy's light, and the presence of any bar-like structure in the galaxy's disk. It also examines the relationship between the nucleus' morphology and the spiral galaxy's disk, the active galactic nucleus (Nuclei) morphology, and any bar-like structure in the galaxy's disk. The study finds that the spiral hosts of the Nuclei are predominantly disk galaxies with well-defined and smooth disks. Most of the Nuclei are located near the center of their host galaxies, and the morphology of the Nuclei is mostly consistent with the morphology of their host galaxies, and the morphology of the Nuclei is mostly consistent with the morphology of any bar-like structure in the galaxy's disk. The study finds that the spiral hosts of the Seyfert galaxies of the Nuclei have a predominant edge-on orientation in comparison to the UNY sample, and the morphology of the Nuclei is mostly consistent with the morphology of any bar-like structure in the galaxy's disk. This paper features two key outcomes: Firstly, we establish a connection between flat general rotational surfaces and a specific classification by their pointwise 1-type Gauss maps; alternatively, we show this relationship yields product surfaces as a consequence. Secondly, we derive all possible 1-type surfaces with constant Gaussian curvature, achieving a complete characterization in this regard.

While top-tier image classification models require substantial manual labeling, 
estimating scene geometry can be achieved through self-supervision, allowing the 
models to utilize unlabelled data for pre-training. As a result, it's more than 
plausible to enhance model performance by pre-training with scene geometry rather 
than traditional image classification. In this research, we propose Efficient 
Depth and Camera Pre-training (EDCP), a novel self-supervised learning algorithm, 
with the primary goal of providing a robust geometric foundation for various 
computer vision research fields. In EDCP, pairwise fundamental matrices are 
initially self-trained, followed by the estimation of camera poses and depths. 
Furthermore, a RANSAC-based pre-processing step filters out low-confidence 
estimates. We also explore different training strategies, such as patch-based and 
image-based approaches, and multi-scale training. Our experimental results show 
that EDCP outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on several 3D estimation 
benchmarks and provides meaningful object-level semantic representations. Our 
pre-trained models and source code are freely accessible at the provided GitHub 
link.

TCube is an advanced training platform for time-series datasets, featuring a comprehensive collection of educational materials and interactive visualizations. It empowers users to develop and train deep learning models for tasks such as classification and anomaly detection. Recognizing the challenges associated with training data scarcity and expert talent shortage in time-series analysis, TCube addresses these issues by offering a collaborative environment and seamless deployment of trained models. TCube's unique design includes a rich dataset of training data, a transparent visualization of timeseries models, and a unified workspace for developing multi-class classifiers and anomaly detectors.

The Ising model on a Cayley tree based on the free product of two groups of different sizes is analyzed using a combination of group theory and symmetry principles. This approach transforms the model into a problem that can be solved exactly using a double-wedge product of representations associated with the two groups. As a result, the double-wedge product turns out to be only partially irreducible, which has significant implications for understanding the Ising model's integrability when applied to regular trees with infinite symmetry.

This research paper outlines a novel application of Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks to enhance Japanese word segmentation accuracy. We have developed a comprehensive dataset comprising approximately 1.2 million Japanese word-segmented lines of text, extracted from various sources, along with corresponding word-level part-of-speech (POS) tags. Our proposed method employs an LSTM-based word-segmentation model that utilizes character-level features, which we have found significantly boosts segmentation accuracy. Additionally, our experiments also demonstrate that the trained model successfully improves the accuracy of word-level POS tagging.

Stack Overflow, established in 2008, has become the leading online platform for programmers to post and resolve queries, accumulating a substantial corpus of over 22 million questions and 36 million answers. While individual responses often incorporate external references, identifying the most frequently shared and reused content remains unclear. This study analyzes references to external content referenced in Stack Overflow discussions from 2009 to 2019 and reveals key insights. Firstly, we investigate the reference sharing behavior of Stack Overflow users and their responses. Secondly, we identify the most frequently shared content by SO users, revealing that programming languages and languages are the primary external resources shared. Furthermore, our research shows that content shared by SO users often experiences a resurgence in popularity, and we explore the underlying reasons for this. Lastly, we demonstrate that popular external content is commonly shared by SO users with a higher reputation. Leveraging a novel dataset comprising Stack Overflow references and user reputation, our study offers a new perspective on reference sharing in online programming communities.

The problem of rotating galactic plains extending over vast distances remains unresolved. We've developed a more comprehensive understanding of this issue by building upon Davis's 1986 research and expanding it with the inclusion of a flat core in the central galactic regions, similar to what is observed in many galaxies today. This model assumes that galactic rotation curves reach a constant speed at the center, resulting from an isothermal core of dark matter. Due to the presence of such dark matter configurations, the distances at which these constant rotational curves begin are significantly lower than previously believed. Our analysis indicates that the outer galactic regions can be accurately described by Davis's original models, even with the inclusion of dark matter's isothermal core. Consequently, the rotational speeds of galaxies without such cores are likely to be even higher than those with cores. Consequently, existing data may not be sufficient to fully rule out Davis's original theories, but it is certain that they are capable of producing the rotation curves observed in galaxies. This conclusion holds regardless of the density of dark matter's isothermal core, which can range from 0.2 to 80 times that of the present day's critical density.

Although climate change attitudes have typically been seen as a barrier, they have also been seen as a potential source of inspiration for generating solutions and fostering action. The challenge is that people's responses to climate change messages often fail to connect with their personal beliefs, which in turn hampers their ability to envision solutions or take meaningful action. This issue can be addressed by incorporating an individual's own values as a framework for classifying climate change attitudes, which can also connect these values to specific solutions and behaviors that align them with the person's own belief system. This research introduces a novel framework that identifies personal values and categorizes climate change attitudes based on those values. By using a diverse set of valued principles, such as truthfulness and respect for nature, our sub-value-based framework accurately identifies individual climate change attitudes and achieves high overall accuracy rates of 86.1% across multiple personal value dimensions.

In healthcare applications, extracting clinical symptoms from unstructured text notes has significant implications. However, limited availability of high-quality clinical natural language processing training data poses a challenge. To address this issue, we conducted a study to demonstrate the effectiveness of domain generalization techniques in symptom extraction within a German clinical environment. Our research involved three approaches, including data augmentation using back-translation and regularization techniques. Additionally, we explored the use of character-level representations to mitigate data scarcity and improve performance, utilizing Character Embedding Layers and Character Embedding Pooling Layers. Our findings show that domain generalization through all techniques substantially enhances symptom extraction performance, while regularizations serve as effective auxiliaries. Furthermore, our experiments reveal that combining domain generalization methods consistently outperforms individual applications and yields robust performance even with minimal training data.

Autonomous vehicles face complex challenges in navigating partial observability, limited field of view, and dynamic environments. Deep neural networks have emerged as a viable solution, yet their potential remains underutilized. To improve the reliability and adaptability of autonomous driving systems, it is essential to learn features that enhance robustness and generalizability. Through an in-depth examination of recent developments and their underlying principles, we aim to shed light on the most effective approaches to feature learning and neural network design for autonomous driving tasks. Our analysis centers on how these networks facilitate learning, comparing their effectiveness and highlighting the need for further investigation. One of the most effective ways to enhance the learning process is by leveraging Recurrent Neural Networks, which excel at handling partial observability and temporal dynamics, particularly in uncertain and changing environments like those encountered in autonomous driving.

Mottled and inverting holistic neural networks (MI-HNNs), a type of pulse-coupled neural network, serve as robust classifiers capable of operating on unlabelled data, while consuming minimal power. This paper introduces the MI-HNN architecture and utilizes it on the MNIST and ILSVRC-2012 datasets to demonstrate its effectiveness. Additionally, MI-HNNs can function as adaptable, nonstationary filters in spatial filtering schemes. We apply the MI-HNNs within the MI-HNN-SFF framework and achieve improved performance on the JMatTorch image classification dataset and the challenging Stride dataset in cross-domain and source-free domain adaptation settings.

In high-energy heavy ion collisions, the simulation of the particle interaction process benefits from modeling the quark behavior under specific conditions. A proposed phase, the spin-polarized strange quark matter, offers a promising approach for this purpose. To accurately predict the density distribution and mean free path of the quark matter, its thermodynamic properties must be established under the collision environment, which is characterized by a high temperature and low equilibrium. A mathematical model for the state equation of the spin-polarized strange quark matter in a magnetic field is developed. Contrary to standard assumptions, the magnetic field's influence on the matter is significant and directly related to the matter density. Furthermore, the matter becomes thermodynamically unstable beyond a certain point (approximately 0.068 fm^-3), which should be taken into account for its application in collision simulations. Lastly, the magnetic field has a substantial softening effect on the matter, particularly at high temperatures and among the spin-down component, potentially decreasing their transport coefficients by a factor of 2 to 3.

The Personal Data Nebula (Pando) is a pioneering approach designed to transform the use of personal devices, enabling them to collaboratively form a unified, secure data environment. As Pando's latest advancement builds upon its foundational work on federated learning enhancements, it further refines the core features of the initial system. Specifically, it boosts computational efficiency by leveraging advanced learning algorithms and peer-to-peer communication techniques, while simultaneously bolstering its resilience through the integration of robust communication protocols. As a result, the average computational throughput has increased to 70%, and the reliability of communication protocols is maintained at an impressive 98.77% success rate.

We integrate an adaptive sampling strategy into a specific Galerkin method for finding eigenvalues and eigenvectors of high-dimensional definite variations that involve high-order derivatives. The outcome is a more efficient numerical method for solving these equations. In our numerical experiments, this method efficiently computes accurate eigenvalues and eigenvectors even in the most demanding cases.

We will investigate a non-integer base representation for various real numbers, focusing on the concept of intermediate transformations, first introduced by Brudnyi, as well as the bases and $\beta$-expansions. Our research involves analyzing the topological properties of the set containing all possible outcomes from these transformations, specifically how this set relates to existing transformations like those of Gr\"obner and Solomyak, and the $\beta$-transformation. Moreover, our findings demonstrate that the topological properties of this set depend on not only the base $\beta$ but also on the intermediate parameter. Notably, the measure zero sets under the unique ergodicity measure can still contain elements with powerful diophantine properties, leading to the discovery of sets composed of badly approximable numbers in non-integer bases with measure zero, which were previously unexplored.

We study SO(Nc) gauge theories with Nf quark flavors using lattice simulations to investigate their confinement properties. The theories exhibit a SU(NF) chiral symmetry that can be broken by quark bilinears with odd parity under C. In the sigma model, this leads to a non-relativistic invariance due to the massive nature of the pseudoscalar mesons. In our research, we examine the theories with Nf = 2 and 3 quark flavors on a 12^4 lattice for several values of the coupling beta, and compare the simulation results to those from SU(2) gauge theories with the same number of quark flavors.

EAC is a new explainability technique akin to Permutation Importance but focused on providing non-linear, high-granularity causal insights from black-box models. Previous work demonstrated the value of Disentangled Attribution Curves (DAC) in generating concise, per-factor explanations that can be used to create factor-specific causal factor graphs. In this post, we provide a brief introduction to Disentangled Attribution Curves and their ability to isolate the impact of individual time-series factors on a target time-series. Furthermore, we apply DAC to a complex bike-sharing dataset and employ the Disentangled Attribution Curve function in PyEx to generate a first pass of factor-specific causal factor graphs. Although EAC and DAC are general-purpose explainability tools suitable for various black-box models, they may suffer from a lack of scalability due to their computational intensity. Future work will focus on developing more scalable causal explainability methods that retain the high fidelity and granularity of EAC while improving scalability.

In the context of federated learning, various approaches have been proposed to ensure the privacy of training data, but most focus on either vertical or horizontal settings, leaving multi-table scenarios largely unexplored in existing solutions. Furthermore, several methods either demand excessive computational resources, rely on too many assumptions, or are susceptible to gradient inversion attacks. To address these challenges, we introduce a general approach that covers both vertical and horizontal federated learning, utilizing differential privacy to protect data. Our solution minimizes assumptions, communication requirements, and computational resources while effectively balancing utility and privacy. We also put forth the first solution for the vertical federated learning scenario that is immune to differential privacy attacks. Comprehensive experimental results validate the utility and privacy properties of our solution in various federated learning settings. The accompanying code and documentation are available for public review at https://github.com/klf-labs/KLF.

We developed a novel drivers testing solution on microcontrollers, allowing for the simultaneous testing of multiple devices. The method involves three key elements: the Driver Under Test (DUT), the Microcontroller Emulator (MCE), and the Personal Computer (PC). The DUT contains the driver software and communicates with the target device, while the PC runs a control program to coordinate the testing process. A single PC with specific software can manage multiple DUTs and MCEs simultaneously,. The DUTs can be configured in-line with each other to reduce the number of required DUTs and MCEs. The testing process begins once the control program loads the data, which is then initiated by sending an interrupt to the target device. This study outlines our approach and results in detail.

This system, called Timeloops, effectively blocks system calls in applications written in interpreted languages like PHP and Python, by leveraging written test cases that specify desired system call outcomes, without requiring any system call system call mocking infrastructure. It builds on previous research by targeting applications developed in these specific interpreted languages, and employs special machine code interpretation techniques to achieve filtering, by directly interpreting a modified version of the target application during execution in hardware or through a hardware accelerator. This approach allows Timeloops to execute specific machine code instructions related to system calls and interpret them in hardware, resulting in an efficient filtering process that does not involve any additional system call infrastructure.

Single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) data analysis is complicated by the presence of high-dimensional sparsity, noise, and large dataset size. We evaluated the effectiveness of various dimensionality reduction and embedding techniques for processing real-world scRNA-seq datasets. Given that most existing methods are designed to function in high-dimensional Euclidean spaces, we investigated the impact of reducing data dimensions before applying these techniques. By using a low-dimensional product space, we found that such a approach yields significant performance improvements for classification and visualization tasks. Furthermore, we found that moving from Euclidean to low-dimensional product spaces also results in substantial performance gains for existing dimensionality reduction methods. In particular, our findings show that classifying cells with k-NN in low-dimensional spaces can outperform classifying in Euclidean spaces by 15-40%. This discovery has important implications for the design of machine learning pipelines for scRNA-seq data processing. To facilitate this, we developed and publicly released the PyTorch-based deep learning algorithms including SPTRL, MLP, and vMLP for classifying and predicting cell types.

For a long time, there has been a debate about whether supermassive black holes (SMBHs) sit at the center of galaxies. We've developed an analytical framework to measure the displacement of these galaxies due to the gravitational pull of their neighboring stars. This analytical approach considers SMBH masses up to $10^7 M_\odot$, varying stellar densities, and different star orbital energies. We've compared our results to N-body simulations for various galaxy models, including those with constant or rising stellar density, and found that our formula accurately predicts displacement rates in these scenarios. We've discovered that in models with a flat mass distribution, where most stars have low energy, the displacement rates are lower than in models with a rising mass distribution, characterized by a low exponential cutoff in the mass function. We've estimated the displacement rates for various SMBH masses and found that for a typical galaxy with a $10^5 M_\odot$ SMBH at its center, the displacement rate is approximately $10^4$ years, making it feasible to observe this phenomenon.

This research introduces a novel method for randomly-modified Model Predictive Control to handle the effects of uncertainty. Utilizing the current state and past information of the system, we develop a novel implementation of stochastic Model Predictive Control that is based on the concept of random-activated events. Our approach involves creating and solving an offline probabilistic safety filter that is designed to manage uncertainty and various types of disturbances. These disturbances are triggered according to a probability distribution that is based on historical data of the system. By using our method, we design and implement stochastic Model Predictive Control without requiring extensive simulations or probability assumptions about the disturbances.

Independent Component Analysis (ICA) is a widely utilized technique in various compression and processing systems for the analysis of large-scale data sets. However, the application of ICA in such systems often leads to a significant increase in memory requirements and processing time. To address this issue, we have introduced two novel methods for performing ICA under compression, utilizing asymptotic behavior as the population size decreases. Our proposed methods leverage the reduced dimensionality to lower memory requirements and processing time, while maintaining high levels of accuracy. We have compared our algorithms to existing compression techniques and have found that they offer a more efficient and accurate alternative.

In an epidemic model known as the asymmetric noisy voter model on a one-dimensional lattice, each site holds a spin that updates its value based on a random selection of its neighbors. If the competition between two types of sites is considered, where each site updates its value based on a random selection of its neighbors, but with an asymmetry in the probability of receiving information from left or right neighbors, the model exhibits different outcomes depending on the parameter values. For low probability values, the competition leads to two possible outcomes: one type of site dominates or the types coexist in equilibrium. The model's behavior near the boundary can be accurately predicted through numerical simulations and is also confirmed through rigorous mathematical analysis.

We investigate a vector state defined on a von Neumann algebra, specifically within the framework of DHR (von Neumann algebra classification, type II_1, quantum spin chains with a single particle, and von Neumann algebras, specifically of type II_1). Given a finitely generated von Neumann algebra, it can be shown that the von Neumann algebra, in the context of ground states with no frustration, has a classification within the range of factors (specifically, of type II_1). This finding has significant implications, demonstrating that local von Neumann algebras, under the specified ground states, adhere to the classification of factors (specifically, of type II_1). The given finding has implications, demonstrating that local von Neumann algebras, under the specified ground states, adhere to the classification of factors (specifically, of type II_1).

A system consisting of two cavities and a set of coherent beamsplitters is analyzed, which facilitates intricate quantum interactions among quantum states. The first cavity's output is fed into the second, creating an entangled output of the remaining cavity modes. The second system's entangled output is fed into the first, completing a quantum loop of the two cavities and beamsplitters. The effect of coherent feedback on entanglement is compared to traditional incoherent methods and individual performance of the two system's components. The method's robustness of generated entanglement against thermal noise is found to significantly exceed that of incoherent methods. The method is also found to produce less entanglement when the input of the system is not in a quantum state but in a mixed quantum state.

A general method is presented for deriving splitting operators at one-loop level for triple-collinear situations, applicable to any number of legs and number of active flavors, with q and qbar as active flavors. The resulting splitting operators are especially relevant for creating subtraction terms in QCD for phase-space integration. Verifications of the operator definition are also provided and its consistency with existing literature is confirmed. Notably, the operator's definition involves and clarifies the relationship between colour-disconnected and colour-connected splitting functions at one-loop level. This work focuses on triple-collinear splitting but can be extended to other types of singularities.

We expand upon Greenberg's strong approximation theorem by adapting it to one-dimensional local rings with residue field of characteristic $p$. This process involves integrating elements from the perfect residue field into the ring in a way that preserves its topological properties. Specifically, we develop methods for lifting elements from the perfect residue field to the ring under the $p$-adic topology. These methods are versatile and applicable across a range of settings, including rigid analytic spaces and $p$-adic Hodge theory.

In recent years, the interest in science policy has been increasing, as evidenced by the rise in its number of publications. This is complemented by the growing enthusiasm for citizen science among the general public. To address the lack of historical scientific documentation in Indonesia, particularly with regard to sundials, an innovative approach utilizing citizen science is being implemented by the University of Brawijaya through an online tool called Suwi. This project aims to capture insights into sundial functionality, history, and orientation through a series of interactive games, as well as a online exhibition. Furthermore, to engage the public, sundial-related events are being organized, including guided tours, gifting kits, and sundial design contests. Through these initiatives, the Sundari and Suwi projects are making significant strides in exploring the rich sundial culture in Indonesia, as well as contributing to the broader understanding of science policy.

This study considers Data and Energy-Information Enabled through Device (DED2D) systems, where satellites and drones assist in transferring data and energy to ground-based devices. To address this, we introduce the Time-Frequency Impulse Energy and Information Transfer (TFIET) approach, a strategy to simultaneously supply data and energy to multiple devices. The TFIET method utilizes beamforming and beamsteering, with the former involving precise targeting and the latter comprising multiple targeted beams over a specific duration. The theoretical framework for data and energy transmission over free-space links underpins the TFIET method. Furthermore, we develop the Optimized TFIET (OPTIET) scheme, which optimizes the transmission duration and power allocation to maximize overall system data and energy transmission. The OPTIET scheme employs a two-stage optimization process, with the first stage solving non-convex optimization using semi-definite programming and the second stage solving linear programming. Simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of the OPTIET scheme, with OPTIET achieving up to 120% and 160% improvements in total data and energy transmission, respectively, compared to existing methods.

The growing emphasis on remote work in various industries has led to a heightened interest in automating complex experimental setups. Although such automated systems have been in use for over 30 years in the semiconductor industry, their application in the life and service sectors remains relatively unknown. This document outlines the process of designing and implementing an automated experimental framework using the ROS Melodic version and Python, with a focus on creating a versatile system that can be customized and expanded upon. Additionally, the paper discusses implementing automated quality control measures and securely integrating the automated framework within a remote work environment, including the use of password protection and encrypted messaging via SSH.

We establish that Asser's conjecture for the class of spectra of undirected bipartite graphs has the same complexity as Angluin's for directed ones. Consequently, bipartite graphs with a linear number of edges can be recognized by linear-sized, unique, directed models, and this result holds even for models with limited transition weights. Furthermore, our finding that Asser's conjecture for bipartite graphs is resolved through the use of directed models represents a substantial increase in understanding compared to the previous proof by linear-sized Rabin-automata.

A detailed computational model has been developed to optimize electrostatic phase plates for improved electron probe performance. By accurately simulating phase plate field and current properties, the model offers a novel approach for designing phase plates that achieve minimum probe size without compromising the current density. The results also highlight an unexpected increase in current density around the phase plate's edge, which can be leveraged to improve probe current convergence. Various designs for a 1 nm probe without field emission are presented, including a square and circular phase plate with different fill factors. Additionally, a 0.42 nm probe with field emission of roughly 10000 e-/s is designed using a 50% fill-factor square phase plate.

We introduce a unified theory describing multiple physical computation methods, including classical, quantum, and thermodynamic approaches. By adapting a successful model for simulating classical and quantum systems, further examples are investigated. One finding reveals that, in the proposed framework, quantum computation is not a separate mechanism. Unlike other evaluation methods, which can be attributed to standard theorems for classical and quantum computation, the framework's assumptions about an all-encompassing system lead to distinct results for the quantum case. Moreover, we demonstrate that the framework enables the description of thermodynamic and thermoelectric computation principles and confirms previous findings in this area. Moreover, our research shows that successful thermal computation is contingent upon specific thermal interactions. These concepts are further illustrated through simplified models and numerical simulations.

Where $X_t$ is a simple random walk on the hypercube of dimension $d$ ($d \geq 3$) and $Y_t$ is a simple random walk on the hypercube of dimension $d+1$, starting from their respective middle points, what is the expected first occurrence time of the count $|x_t - y_t| = b$ for a given odd integer $b \geq 1$?

In our research, we explore a polymer black hole, which is modeled using the polymer Hamiltonian constraint, and investigate its physical properties in detail. We represent this polymer black hole as a wormhole with a geometric throat, which is located at the point of maximum spatial curvature, and compare its physical properties to those of the Schwarzschild black hole. We examine the distribution of the wormhole's energy-momentum tensor and the amount of exotic matter required, as well as the behavior of tidal forces experienced by travelers passing through the throat. We analyze the Riemann curvature invariants, the geodesic completeness, and the thermal properties of the wormhole, including its radiation spectrum, which can be detected by observers at the throat. We demonstrate that, due to the behavior of the tangent bundle, there is no sign of singularity at the throat, and the curvature, energy, and tidal forces tend towards finite and non-zero values as they approach the region of the classical Schwarzschild radius. We investigate the energy-momentum components, which reveal that, for sufficiently large masses, the amount of exotic matter required is relatively small and localised near the throat. We examine the tidal forces and find that, for sufficiently large masses, the forces are within human survivability. We represent the interior of the black hole as a wormhole, where the required energy violates minimal energy conditions, and the mass of the required exotic matter is smaller than the black hole mass near the throat, especially for larger masses

The linear renormalization of the quasiparticle velocity in doped graphene is explored through numerical simulations, utilizing the stochastic light-front approach. This research examines how the quasiparticle velocity is influenced by various levels of doping. By imposing the Ward-Takahashi identity on the self-energy's scalar and vector components, the numerical results demonstrate a monotonic decrease in specific heat and a distinct maximum in the thermal wind speed as a function of doping. These findings are supported by the analytical predictions of previous studies.

A newly developed system called MaskedSpeech learns speech synthesis with a novel approach that combines speech transformation and cutting-edge speech synthesis techniques. By embedding speech segments obtained from the former into a model-based system while fine-tuning it with back-propagation, this system significantly improves the naturalness and expressiveness of synthesized speech while reducing computational complexity. Experimental findings on the LJ-Maid dataset reveal that this system achieves an 11.3 dB improvement in the MOS score with minimal computational requirements, as well as superior performance in voice conversion and mask learning with state-of-the-art models.

High-dimensional regression analysis based on Bayesian quantile regression analysis has received relatively little attention. This study introduces a streamlined and efficient approach for selecting posterior variables in quantile regression analysis within the context of high-dimensional datasets. The proposed method incorporates a novel Grouping Correlated Model (GCM) that arranges the posterior inclusion probabilities of individual variables into distinct groups based on their correlation structure, while also reducing the number of variables within each group to a single representative variable. This technique not only maintains the posterior uncertainties of the original model but also enhances the stability of variable selection. A Monte Carlo Carlo Markov Chain algorithm is employed to estimate the joint posterior distribution of parameters and indicator variables under the GCM. The effectiveness and performance of this approach are evaluated through the use of two real-world datasets.

This paper examines different types of attacks and defensive strategies against deep learning networks, contrasting traditional adversarial examples with new Man-in-the-Middle attacks. A comparison of several methods for generating adversarial examples, such as input manipulation and adding noise, is conducted. Through experiments on three diverse classifiers and benchmark datasets, it's demonstrated that some techniques robust against test data manipulations may be vulnerable to novel attacks. The man-in-the-middle can introduce novel examples into a DNN's output without accurately manipulating the original input data. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis on how these attacks and defensive measures can be used against deep learning networks, providing a roadmap for further research in this field.

Current research indicates growing climate change denial among Americans, and emerging data suggest rising concern and support for the environment among Gen Z. We conducted a study to comprehend how conspiracy theories regarding climate change are spreading on AMT through examining climate change deniers' (CCDs) sharing patterns of conspiracy theories from 2019 to 2021. Our research employed an NLP-based approach to classify whether the AMT data contained climate change-related conspiracy theories using a pretrained language model. We then analyzed the AMT conspiracy deniers' network, identifying their most influential members and their shared topics. Influential members were those with the greatest impact in spreading conspiracy theories, either by posting themselves or sharing content from others. We found that conspiracy theories are widely shared among AMT users and that certain members have more frequently shared these theories than others. The majority of conspiracy theories are shared by members with large follower counts. Furthermore, our results revealed that conspiracy theory-related content is actively circulated by conspiracy deniers and that their most active members have significantly high follower counts. The majority of conspiracy deniers are associated with QAnon, a conspiracy theory movement on AMT. We found that conspiracy deniers frequently share posts promoting globalist agendas, COVID-19 denials, vaccination fears, and climate change, with conspiracy deniers with the highest follower counts tending to focus more on general topics such as globalism and COVID-19.

Researchers from the CMS collaboration analyzed proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV energy using data collected between 2016 and 2018. A search for particular patterns of a particular type of particle interaction was conducted, specifically looking for the association of a particular type of particle interaction with the production of jets and missing energy. A total of 136,676 proton-proton collisions were analyzed and 97,891 of these were consistent with what was expected. The number of actual collisions recorded was 13.7 what was expected. The results showed no statistically significant deviation from the standard model, leading to new restrictions on the theoretical models explaining the interaction of certain types of particles. The analysis also includes the development of certain types of particles known as vector-like quarks and the production of dark matter particles. The analysis was carried out independently of the type of particle involved, specifically the production of a certain type of particle known as a vector-like quark and the production of dark matter particles.
